In this very place, the non-dualistic doctrine of the Lord (Īśvarādvaitavāda), having attained perfect consistency through the path of correct reasoning taught by the excellent gurus beginning with the venerable Somānandanātha, has been brought under one's own control.

Spreading forth from Kashmir with its manifest fragrance and delighting all people of every land, it attained a state of universal veneration never before seen in any other region, like the diffusion of saffron. || 1 ||
Cross swiftly the ocean of saṃsāra; establish your feet immovably in the supreme state, which is overflowing with the joy of eternal light.
Contemplate within yourself the nectar-essence of the realization of non-duality taught by Śiva, through the forceful manifestation of immediate reasoning.
which bestows a sense of upliftment. || 2 ||
Now follows the Determination of the Pulsations (Spanda-nirṇaya), composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja.

She who always projects everything from the earth up to Śiva— whose own nature is her very self— upon the wall of her own independent and pure self, like a city in a mirror, from her own essential form.

Victorious in the world is that Spanda-śakti of Śaṅkara, who is the Goddess of Vision, the potency of mantra, eternally arisen, full of the nature of the mass of sounds, and the infinite radiance of the "Hanta! [or "Nanda! exclamation. || 1 ||
Even though the nectar of vibration has been tasted slightly through the abundance of vibrations, I have undertaken this effort toward the full enjoyment of that tasting. (2)

If you desire to know the Upaniṣad of Śiva— the perfect consistency of the Sūtras, the thorough comprehension of the supreme reality, the highest and sharp discourse on reasoning, the application of skillful means, and the clear exposition of the true meaning— then [seek it].
O wise ones, fix your minds upon this commentary on the Śrī Spandaśāstra; may you attain the splendor of Spanda. || 3 ||

For here, the illustrious teacher Vasuguptācārya— whose greatness was manifested through the immersion into the supreme Śiva who desires to favor the entire universe, and who received instruction as if in a dream—
[attained this] from Mount Mahādeva solely by the will of the Blessed Lord.
Having obtained the *Śivasūtras*— the most secret teachings inscribed upon a great stone slab— he composed this work,

comprising fifty-one verses that are both lucid and profound, demonstrating the unification of scripture, personal experience, and logical reasoning. Therein, the first twenty-five [verses] concern the vibration of one's true nature (*svarūpaspanda*), and the next seven...
The *Sahajavidyodayaspanda* (the vibration of the arising of innate knowledge) is the nineteenth; thus, the *Vibhūtispanda* (the vibration of manifestation) has been described.

Therefore, this *Spandaśāstra* consists of three outpourings (*niṣyanda*). In this first outpouring, the subject matter of the treatise is introduced by means of a verse preceded by praise. Then, by means of four verses, [it is explained] with supporting arguments.
The principle of *spanda* has been established. Then, by means of two verses, the means for attaining that [state] is stated along with its identifying characteristics.

By one verse, misconceptions regarding the means are dispelled. By another verse, the very means is reinforced through the description of its conformity with the attainment of the goal (*upeya*). Following that, by one [verse], that which is obtainable through those means—
The nature of that which is to be attained has been demonstrated; therefore, by relying upon that, the absence of saṃsāra has been stated in the verse.

By refuting the view of the proponents of non-existence with two verses, the distinctiveness of the *spanda* principle from that [view] has been explained. And by one verse, although the effect manifested by that [principle] is perishable...
That is designated as "inexhaustible. Having established this very point through two verses, the doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvavāda*) has been uprooted.

Then, by one [verse], it is made known that this is attained at all times by the *suprabuddha* (the perfectly awakened one), whereas for the *prabuddha* (the awakened one), it occurs at the prior and posterior limits. By another [verse], the distinction of the objects of perception for the *suprabuddha* is stated.

Then, by another [verse], the reasoning for the absence of obscuration in one who is perfectly awakened (*suprabuddha*) was presented. By a [further] verse, it was stated that the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the unawakened is concealed. Thereafter, by one [verse], it was said that one must constantly exert effort in order to attain the state of perfect awakening.
By a [final] verse, it was shown that certain states of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-avasthā*) themselves consist in the cessation of all other mental functions; such is the nature of exertion.

The object [of the teaching] has been explained. Furthermore, by means of the three verses beginning with "yasyonmeṣa" and ending with "prabuddhaḥ syādanāvṛtaḥ," it is stated that one who has attained awakening must remain vigilant (*prajāgaritavyam*) in order to achieve perfect awakening—that is, to shatter the veil of darkness belonging to the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) which is appropriate for that stage. Now, [the following]:

We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the power-circle (śakticakra), by whose opening and closing of his eyes the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur, and whose meaning we shall now explain in this treatise. || 1 ||

We praise Śaṅkara, who is the non-dual nature of one's own consciousness consisting of supreme bliss and the complete pacification of all afflictions; perceiving him as the preeminent excellence of the universe, we enter into him by immersing ourselves in the state of the subject fashioned by him.

For it is precisely that immersion (*samāveśa*) which is taught in this treatise as the fruit of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). The plural number is used to manifest the non-difference of all those to be graced, who are glanced upon by the eye of grace.
By the phrase "of him" (*yasya*), the author proclaims that which was hinted at by the word "him" (*tam*)—namely, his state of being beyond all commonality. Here [in this verse]:

The Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, whose essence is light, because his core consists of the reflective awareness of the supreme *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness) which is the ultimate reality of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), is eternally of the nature of a vibration consisting of a solid mass of bliss; he is the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) who is the friction-stick (*araṇi*) for the two-fold emission (*visarga*).

The power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), though undivided, displays the entire succession of emanation, withdrawal, and so forth—like a city in a mirror—upon its own surface; by means of the logic of what is to be, it makes that which is not distinct appear as if it were distinct.
Because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *spand* (to vibrate) in the sense of a slight movement, it is called "vibration" (*spanda*); therefore, the Lord is eternally [this vibration].

The true essence is the reality of *spanda* (vibration), not non-vibration; for some have said that the supreme reality is non-vibration (*aspanda*). For if it were so, then because its nature would be quiescent, this [reality] would be devoid of lordship (*anīśvara*).
This [text], however, is intended precisely to establish one's own essential nature as Śaṅkara, which consists of the power of *spanda* whose core is radiant manifestation (*sphurattā*).
The treatise titled *Samucitaspanda* was composed by the Great Gurus;
this shall become clear [later].

And this very power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) consists of the wonder of "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*), which is of the nature of bliss, wherein the creation and withdrawal of all things are internalized within.
She whose true nature is the manifestation of the contraction and expansion of the subject and object in their entirety—both pure and impure;

she who is to be worshipped by all the Upaniṣads; she who consists simultaneously of both opening and closing [of the eyes]; for she is the form of the destroyer of the entire aggregate of principles (tattva), from Śiva down to the earth, which was previously created.
The very ground of the closing of the eyes (nimeṣa) is the state of the Creator with respect to the future manifestation;

likewise, the ground of the opening of the eyes (unmeṣa) is the ground of the closing of the eyes of the universe, which is the mass of consciousness (ciddhana) whose essence is the opening [of manifestation]. Furthermore, the ground of immersion into the mass of consciousness is itself the form of the universal opening, according to the scripture.
The Goddess is eternally licking [the world], and she shines forever full;
she is the wave of the ocean of consciousness, the power whose essence is the will of the Lord.
Thus, the illustrious Maheśvara, by means of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*),

assumes the levels of subjects ranging from Śiva, Mantramaheśvara, Mantreśvara, Mantravijñānākala, Pralayākala, to Sakala, as well as the levels of their respective objects of cognition, while retaining the nature of each preceding stage.

Although it remains as the foundational wall, by the play of concealing its own essential nature, it causes [the lower levels] to close while simultaneously causing them to open; through the process of descent, it causes each successive form to close, whereas through the process of ascent,
it causes each successive form to open for those yogins of knowledge.

For this very reason, each subsequent form causes the preceding one to abandon its nature of contraction and manifest as expansion; conversely, each preceding form causes the subsequent one to submerge its state of expansion and appear in a contracted form. In this way, He manifests everything as being composed of everything.

Let this suffice for now: this perception of duality exists merely due to the contraction projected by that [consciousness], and the teaching here is intended precisely to uproot it. Furthermore, even though consciousness consists of the unfolding manifestation (*unmeṣa*) of appearances such as blue or pleasure, its nature—which is essentially one with the subject—is characterized by the closing of the eyes (*nimeṣa*), which consists in the withdrawal of appearances such as yellow that have previously been manifested.

Let those of great intelligence investigate the Blessed Pratibhā for the sake of severing the cycle of transmigration; for this very reason, in his own commentary on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*, the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa [uses] the expression "by means of opening and closing" [of the eyes] as a mere conceptualization.
Thus, it has been explained as being indeed undivided, in the form of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). The author of the *Saṃgraha* also [states]:
"Because for one intent upon a single thought, there arises the emergence of another."
"That [state] is to be known as *unmeṣa* (the opening); one should recognize it for oneself.

(3.9) Here, it will be explained that *unmeṣa* is precisely the withdrawal of commenced thought, which is the cause for the emergence of the supreme nature (*parasvarūpa*), because without the withdrawal of active thought, there is no emergence of the supreme nature. And this is stated in that very same [text]:
We shall expand upon this:
"The descent of the supreme nectar occurs for him through that which arises from conditions;
by means of that, he attains a state of non-independence, and that [descent] has the subtle elements as its object. (3.14)
In this regard as well, it will be stated quite clearly that even arising has the ultimate reality of dissolution:
"When agitation is dissolved, then there would be the supreme state" (1.9).
Here too, it will be demonstrated that the *nimeṣa* (closing), which consists of the dissolution of agitation, is itself the nature of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the supreme state.

Thus, although this single power possesses both forms, it is sometimes designated as predominating in expansion (*unmeṣa*) and sometimes as predominating in contraction (*nimeṣa*). Consequently, from that cause— the power which, while belonging to [the Lord], consists essentially in the contraction of His own nature, yet predominates in the expansion of effects— the entire universe of the world [emerges].

The emergence of [the universe] from Śiva down to the earth is a creation characterized by differentiation, possessing manifold variety, whose true nature consists in the immersion into the essence of non-duality.

Conversely, the dissolution of the world— which is the closing of the eyes of the power that predominates externalization— is the opening of one's own essential nature, a withdrawal of the state of diverse differentiated forms into a manifestation consisting of non-duality.

It should be explained that dissolution is also of the nature of emergence, and emergence is also of the nature of dissolution. In reality, however, nothing at all emerges or perishes; rather, it is the power of vibration (spanda-śakti) alone—the divine, which is itself beyond succession—that, while manifesting as various appearances, seems to emerge and seem to perish. This we shall demonstrate.
Since maintenance, dissolution, and grace consist essentially of specific forms of dissolution and emergence, there is no addition [to the categories];
thus, the fivefold sovereign activity of the Supreme Lord is subsumed within dissolution and emergence alone. And such a matter has been determined in this manner.

[The reading is "evaṃ prāk" (thus previously). This was stated by me myself in the *Spandasandoha*, which is a commentary on the very first aphorism. Now, one might object: "According to the vision of the venerable *Mahārtha*, the diverse dissolutions and arisings of the world are accomplished by the deities of creation and so forth; how then can it be said that [the world belongs] 'to whom' and so on? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Regarding the phrase "the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers": the wheel of powers refers to the assembly of twelve goddesses, such as Sṛṣṭiraktā and the others; its "manifestation" (*vibhava*) consists of the display of play (*krīḍāḍambara*) characterized by exertion, illumination, relishing, and dissolution; [the text identifies the Lord] as the source, that is, the cause, of that manifestation. These...

For it is the traditional teaching (āmnāya) that the Goddesses, having embraced the glorious Manthānabhairava, the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara), perpetually accomplish the play of the creation and so forth of the universe. Furthermore, in response to the doubt as to why the Supreme Lord is the cause of the creation, destruction, and other processes of the universe, this very point is the answer.
[The reading is: "The wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*). For whatever extent anything in the universe arises, it consists of light because it is manifest;
thus, there is the manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Self of the Lord.
"Indeed it exists; without that, the reflective awareness of desire does not proceed" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.10).

According to this principle established by the wise, that which exists as the internal manifestation of the Supreme Lord through identity with His Light alone is called the *sac-chakti-cakra* (the wheel of the powers of Being), from which [all proceeds].
In the scriptures of the Supreme Lord, His possession of infinite power is proclaimed;

He is the source, the cause, of the manifestation of that wheel of powers— the manifold and infinite variety of the universe’s appearances, consisting of its mutual conjunctions and disjunctions, which constitute its ultimate reality.

For that very Blessed One, by uniting and separating the various manifestations of the universe—which consist of the body of consciousness and abide in identity with His own self—through their mutual manifold diversity, is the cause of the emergence and dissolution of the universe. As it has been said: [g: the reading is *tadetad*].
The venerable Bhaṭṭakallaṭa [states] that the sovereignty of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which consists of the body of consciousness (*vijñānadeha*), is the cause of origination.
This is consistent with the words of the commentary in both of these two interpretations. Moreover:
"The entire universe is his power"— according to the perspective of the scriptures,
therefore, in the contemplation of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva. (2.4)
Thus, according to the principle established here, the Sky-farer (Khecarī) of the world-soul resides above on the upward path within the void that is the domain of Vāmeśī;
and according to the secret doctrine, she is of the nature of Vāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī— by me alone.
"In the *Spandasandoha*, that which has been correctly determined [therein],
these [powers]— whose intellects are unawakened— are intent upon concealing their own state" (1.20);
this also applies here.
Since this group of instruments belongs to that which is about to be determined, and which consists of the expansion of the wheel of powers explained by these two commentaries;
thus, [it exists] as the nature of the collection of senses in the state of persistence.
"Having seized that power, the mantras [act]...
Thus, regarding the group of powers (*śaktivarga*) arising from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), which is the eternal essence of mantra—[what is its function]? (3.13)
According to this principle— [the reading "dṛṣṭyā" is found in manuscript G]—

the power (*vibhava*) of the wheel of energies (*śakticakra*), which consists of the very nature of deities such as Brāhmī and others, and which exists in infinite modes such as these, has been extensively determined by me alone in the *Spandasandoha*.
"Prabhava" means that majesty prevails there; it is independent (*svatantra*), not dependent on another like a bound soul (*paśu*).

It refers to that from which there is an origin, a rising, or a manifestation, arising from the "vibhava"—the inward-turned expansion—of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which is a mass of rays (where the reading *svaraśmicakrasya* is found).
The meaning is that through the *bahuvrīhi* [compound], by means of effortlessly beholding the nature of that [reality] which is inward-turned,

there occurs the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the essential nature of the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, it is by the opening and closing— the unfolding and the withdrawal— of the Self, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss, that its own nature is revealed or concealed.

By the principle that "what is within is without," the dissolution and emergence of the universe— which, as the body, is associated with that [inner reality]— occur respectively as its immersion and emergence;
this is the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which is the expansion of the deity of supreme consciousness.

We praise Śaṅkara, who reveals the true nature of those who possess devotion; likewise, we praise Him from whose own self the emergence of the world arises through the unfolding (unmeṣa) consisting of the outward-turning of consciousness, and whose dissolution occurs through the closing (nimeṣa) consisting of the inward-turning— and [we praise] that Greatness of the Goddess, which is the consciousness whose very nature is the unfolding and other activities such as the creation of the universe.

The phrase "we praise Śaṅkara, the cause," should be applied as far as possible. Although the Supreme Lord is entered into the body and so forth, He effects the creation and withdrawal of the world—consisting of the fivefold objects such as form—by means of the opening and closing of the senses. As it has been said by the knower of the secret reality:

"Thus, even in the realm of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the Lord, entering the body and so forth, may by His will manifest externally the very mass of objects already shining within. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.6.7).
Having thus [stated] that it is by His power of sovereignty (*svātantrya-śakti*) that He assumes such objects... [the text continues].
Regarding the statement "by whose opening and closing [of the eyes]," which was thus described by the Guru, here the praise of Śaṅkara takes the form of a state of immersion (*samāveśa*).

The compound *śakticakravibhavātprabhaḥ*—meaning "he whose source is from the manifestation of the wheel of powers"—is a *bahuvrīhi*; it indicates that the expansion of the wheel of powers is the means for attaining him. Thus, the manifestation of the wheel of powers is stated to be the means for its attainment.
The fruit is stated by means of the *tatpuruṣa* compound as "the source and illuminator for those possessing devotion to the expansion of the deity who is supreme consciousness. As he will say:
"From that, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel" (3.19).
Thus, the relationship between the subject matter and the means is the relationship of the goal and the means;
by this very aphorism, the subject matter, the means, the relationship, and the purpose have been set forth. || 1 ||
Now, what is the proof for the existence of Śaṅkara’s nature as such?

Furthermore, from what material cause does he produce the universe without a cause such as an upādāna; and if he himself were the material cause, the universe would obscure him just as a pot obscures a lump of clay. And regarding the state of being obscured or unobscured—

To remove these doubts— namely, that there would be a difference in the nature of the Blessed One, that a cause for his re-emergence must be sought, and that the arising of the world would entail the consequence of duality— he says [the following] with a single stroke:
In that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged,
there is no cessation anywhere because its nature is unobstructed.

For this very Śiva-nature, which is a mass of light and bliss and is one’s own essential being, there is no obstruction—no impediment to its expansion—in any place, time, or form, because its nature is unobscured and its essence is never veiled. This is the sense here: In this [world]...

Whatever may be conceived as obscuring the light of consciousness—be it the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), pleasure, blue, or the like—if that were not manifest, nothing at all would exist;
but since it is indeed manifest, it is of the very nature of Śaṅkara, whose essence is light. Thus, what could obstruct what, or what is the meaning of obstruction?
He establishes this very point— that "this belongs to that"— by means of the qualification beginning with "where," and so forth:

How could there be a cessation of that [consciousness] by itself, wherein— in its own nature as the essence of consciousness— this entire universe, consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, resides as an effect, and which, being manifested by its own light, attains its existence?
For if that were to cease, that which is considered the "ceaser" itself would not manifest; this is the intended meaning of the remainder [of the verse].
As it has been said:
"How could there be restraint by the vital breath for that which consists of that very [breath] itself? (*Ajadapramātṛprakaraṇa* 23).

Thus [ends] the *Ajada-pramātṛ-siddhi*. Now, one might ask: "Granted that there is a manifestation consisting of the persistence of what has arisen, but from where does its very arising come? To this he says: "And because [the world] has emerged from [it]," and so forth. Through the observation of memory, dreams, mental constructs, and the yogic creation, the self-experience of consciousness (*cit*) is established.

Having abandoned the status of being the cause of the world—which is both without proof and logically untenable—it is not appropriate to postulate [the existence of] primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth. By the word "effect" (kārya), this very point is implied; for an effect is defined as that which is produced by the action of an agent, and not otherwise.

It arises immediately after an insentient cause, because it is impossible for an insentient thing to function as a cause, according to the principle stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* [the reading "nyāyāt" is found in manuscript kh]. And this pair of states will be described here under the terms "effect" and "agency": "And here, these two states are designated as 'effect' and 'agency'. (1.14)

In this context, by the word "all" (*sarva*), the independence of the agent from material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth is implied. Furthermore, an effect such as a jar is never observed to conceal the essential nature of its maker, such as a potter. [Objection:
But emergence occurs for that which was previously situated; therefore, does this [effect] exist somewhere at the very beginning, rather than being situated elsewhere? [Reply: Indeed, it is not.

He says "where it is situated" (*yatra sthitam*) with reference to that very same conscious self (*cidātman*). This should also be applied by way of repetition. The meaning is this: if the world did not exist within the conscious self as non-different from the manifestation of the "I," how could it arise from that [self] independently of material causes and the like? Since, however—

"Just as a great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of a banyan tree, so too does this entire world of moving and non-moving beings exist within the seed of the Heart. According to the established tradition of the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*), [this is stated].

And by the reasoning previously stated in the passage, "Of the Lord who is established in the self" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.10), it is established that [the universe] exists there as flashing forth non-differently from Him; therefore, it is logical that this Lord, whose nature is consciousness, causes the world—which is essentially the solidification of His own aesthetic essence (*rasa*)—to emerge. And thus, wherever...

The construction here is: "Because it has emerged while remaining exactly as it was. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of *eva* (only/exactly) and its position is displaced. Now, one might object:
"If this world has emerged from that whose nature is light (*prakāśavapus*), it would not be manifest; for it is illogical that something external to manifestation could be manifested.
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "Because, although it has emerged, it remains right where it was," by repeating the phrase.
It is "conjoining" (*saṃgamanīya*). The particle *ca* has the sense of "also" (*api*) and is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). This is what is meant:

it is not that the pouch or the like, or the walnut and so forth, have emerged from that [source]; rather, it is the Blessed Lord himself who, through his own sovereignty, manifests the form of the universe as if it were distinct, even though it is not distinct from him.

He remains manifesting [the world] upon his own wall like a city in a mirror. Now, let it be granted that the world is unobstructed during the states of emanation and maintenance; however, how is it that this [world] is not concealed by the state of withdrawal, which consists of non-existence and is akin to deep sleep, pertaining as it does to the world? For the object of perception [cannot exist]...
The answer—repeated as "the conscious self (cidātman) is something" and "without the world, there is no grasper"—is this very same point:

because even though the world has emerged from it, and even when produced, it remains situated in that very place; and during the state of dissolution, it abides in identity with that alone, for there is no other destruction of it in the form of a void, since, according to the reasoning to be stated later, it [merges] into the Light.
The meaning is that it is like a wall, because without it [the subsequent state] would be impossible. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda-śāstra*:
"That which is called 'non-empty' is emptiness, and emptiness is said to be non-existence (*abhāva*).
That non-existence is to be understood as the Goddess, wherein all existents have come to their end. [4.292]

Thus, for that in whom everything exists as an effect, which shines only by means of his own light, and even when withdrawn remains in identity with that very light—for him, no such thing as space, time, or form can logically serve as a restrictor. Therefore, he is all-pervasive, eternal, and variegated by the power of the universe (viśvaśakti). [Note: The reading "āvṛttyā" appears in manuscript *kh*.]

Since this reality is self-luminous and established from the very beginning, no miserable means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— which consists in the illumination of an unknown object— is applicable, useful, or even possible for its establishment; on the contrary,
the establishment of the entire universe, including the means of valid cognition and so forth, is dependent upon the establishment of this reality.
As it has been said by our Guru in that *Āloka*: "Even those means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) which extend life to objects—their supreme life-force is that very Supreme Lord. (Tantrāloka 1.55).

Thus: although this world has emerged from that [Reality], it remains situated therein; although it shines by means of His light, it remains as it is, situated within Him; and although it is of the single nature of His light, it is only His light itself which, when perceived directly for the sake of its own realization, appears as such—and not some other thing called "the world. Herein, where...

The word "sthitam" (established) should be repeated and applied twice. Thus, it is established by one's own experience that this reality—which manifests as the union of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal, and which performs what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish—is at all times and in all places unobstructed. As it has been said by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva:
"O Lord of All, your unprecedented Supreme Lordship triumphs, in that it is devoid of anything to be ruled;

yet another [Lordship] of yours likewise exists, by which this world appears, though it does not appear as it truly is. (Uttara-stotra 16). For here, the very world that appears—being reduced to nothing more than its own manifestation—is not distinct from that manifestation.

The meaning is that "something appears. Furthermore, by the statement "where it is situated," which refers to the state of cessation (*upaśama*), and by the phrase "from where it has emerged," which refers to the state of expansion (*prasara*), the yogi—being intent on absorption into his own true nature (*svabhāva*)—must remain so even in both types of samādhi: that of closing and that of opening, since there is no obstruction for him therein. As will be said:
"When agitation is dissolved, then there shall be the supreme state. (1.9) Likewise:
"Therefore, among the reflections on words and their meanings, there is no state that is not Śiva. (2.4)

And furthermore: when there exists some cognizer, such as a Buddhist or another who propounds non-self, and when there exists some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that is considered a sublater, there is no cessation—that is, no negation—of that [non-self].
For if that which negates it and the means of valid cognition that negates it were not established, this would be a marvel without a wall; yet its establishment [is indeed required].

By the very fact that it "shines forth," the Blessed One exists as an eternally established, self-luminous form; this is so even though it has been stated by means of non-verbal [negation] for the purpose of refuting that [notion].
However, it is not that which is the inward-turned state. [1.16]

In this context, by thus declaring that the reality (tattva) of Śiva— which transcends the universe, consists of the universe, and performs the creation, withdrawal, and so forth of the universe— is one's own essential nature (svabhāva), [the author shows] that whatever is to be worshipped among all the supreme lordly [principles] is not superior to this Spanda-reality; it is merely [this very reality] through the power of its own sovereignty (svātantrya).
The diversity of its worship is thus manifested;
in reality, however, this entire [universe] is nothing but the essence of its potency. As he will say:
"Having seized that power, mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One. [2.1]
This has also been demonstrated by way of a stylistic turn. And thus, there is no room for the aforementioned objection.

In this manner, regarding these *Śrī Spanda Sūtras*, which are like wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), that which was explained by all other commentators [the reading *vṛttikṛdbhiḥ* is found in manuscript *kh*].

Furthermore, regarding whatever we have explained here, let those who possess discernment investigate the internal points for themselves— free from envy and free from arrogance— but we do not reveal and demonstrate them at every step, lest the work become overly prolix. || 2 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that such a nature is not experienced during states such as waking? And if this [nature] is not obstructed by anyone through the aforementioned arguments, then it will cease of its own accord during the waking and other states. Anticipating this doubt, the author instructs the one who fails to comprehend even what has already been stated, thereby awakening him: [The text continues: "If it were so, then why is it that the Lord does not manifest His own nature to Himself? For if He did not perceive His own nature, He would not be omniscient; and if He were not omniscient, He would not be the Lord. Therefore, He must indeed perceive His own nature. Furthermore, if He perceives His own nature, then how can there be any obstruction to that perception? Indeed, no one is capable of obstructing the perception of one's own nature. Hence, the Lord’s perception of His own nature is eternal and unobstructed. To explain: the Lord, being the supreme master of all, is free from all defects and endowed with all perfections. If He did not perceive His own nature, He would lack omniscience; and if He lacked omniscience, He could not be the Lord. Therefore, He necessarily perceives His own nature. Moreover, since no one is capable of obstructing the perception of one's own nature, the Lord’s perception of His own nature is eternally unobstructed. Thus, the Lord is always conscious of His own nature. Consequently, the objection that His nature is not perceived during waking and other states is refuted. This is because the Lord’s nature is eternally manifest and cannot be suppressed by any means whatsoever. Therefore, the Lord is eternally self-luminous and eternally aware of His own nature. This concludes the instruction intended to dispel the doubt of one who fails to grasp this point.
Even as it extends through the various states such as waking and the rest, which are non-different from it,
it never departs from its own essential nature as the perceiver.

The word *jāgrat* (waking) is synonymous with *jāgara* (vigilance), as it is so used by the learned. While the distinctions between waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are well-known in the world— or even while those forms consisting of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* recognized by yogis are unfolding and flowing in various different modes— it is, by implication, that very reality which does not deviate from its own nature.

Furthermore, it never departs from its own nature as the self of all, which is the form of the experiencer. For if it were to cease of its own accord, then even the waking state and so forth, being deprived of its illumination, would not manifest anything at all.
Moreover, this subjectivity of its own is established through one's own self-awareness in both the waking and dreaming states for everyone.

Although that [consciousness] is not perceived in the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), it is nevertheless established by the impossibility of accounting for the subsequent memory; moreover, by its very nature as the perceiver, it does not cease. As for the objects of perception, such as the states [of consciousness], let them cease at will through the power of that [consciousness]; what loss is there in this? The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also."

The meaning is that even in the absence of that [distinction], the sequence does not cease. The reason for the distinction between waking and so forth is provided by way of its qualifiers; "in that which is non-different from that" means because it manifests as non-different from that nature of Śiva, it is of the nature of Light. And how can that which is of a single essence [be otherwise]?

Upon the cessation of that [state], he remains. Alternatively, *tat* (that) is the subject word; however, the term *abhinna* (undivided) indicates that the state of being undivided belongs solely to Śiva with respect to waking and the other states. Consequently, even while the distinctions of waking and so forth prevail—that is, while diversity unfolds and assumes its manifold forms—that very essence does not deviate from its own nature; this is how the passage should be construed.

Furthermore, in order to refute the views held by the Sāṃkhyas, Pāñcarātrikas, Grammarians, and others— who maintain that this distinction between waking and other states is either a transformation (pariṇāma) or an illusory manifestation (vivarta)— it has been stated that [the world] is non-different from that [consciousness].
If even the manifold array of states were to exceed pure consciousness in the slightest degree by way of being a transformation, then the nature of consciousness [would be compromised].
Or, if it were to be slightly exceeded in that transformation, then nothing at all would be produced; thus, there is no such thing as transformation. As it has been said:
"Transformation is not possible for either the insentient or the sentient."

Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Kiraṇa*. Nor is it tenable to say that "vivarta" (illusory manifestation) consists in the assumption of a false, differentiated, and other form, because if that which appears were unreal, it would follow that even the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*) would likewise be unreal.
Furthermore, by this [explanation], the Lord’s capacity to accomplish the most difficult tasks is indeed intimated; for [He brings about] the differentiation of waking and the other states.

And therein it reveals its own non-difference; thus, by way of difference, by way of non-difference, and by way of both—through the nature of the triad of powers known as the lower, the higher-lower, and the highest—[it manifests]. (Note: *g* reads "ubhayamekhanātmanā" for "ubhayātmanā").

"It throbs" means that the Lord himself throbs as the essence of the unsurpassed reality of the Trika (the "six-and-a-half"). Therefore, it is taught that even while abiding in states such as waking, he who gathers [this experience] by thus constantly cultivating his own true nature is indeed Śaṅkara himself. || 3 ||

Now, those Buddhists who maintain that the continuum of cognition alone is reality, asserting: "We perceive this very single nature of consciousness as a manifestation in various forms such as joy and sorrow"; and those who hold that the Self is the object of the notion of "I," which is always obscured by adjuncts such as pleasure and so forth; [these are the ones being refuted].
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain [the existence of a self], but he refutes them with a single verse:
"The cognitions 'I am happy,' 'I am miserable,' and 'I am attached,' and so forth, clearly occur in something other than the states of happiness and the rest, which persist throughout [them]. (4)

That very same person who is happy is also the one who is unhappy; because of being joined with passion that lies latent as pleasure, he is "attached," and because of the connection with hatred that lies latent as suffering, he is "hating"— such cognitions (*saṃvidaḥ*) or knowledges exist "elsewhere," namely, in the substrate of states, which is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).

They proceed within that very inward-turned state and clearly rest there, having made it their own direct witness. Otherwise, since momentary cognitions are exhausted in themselves alone, the conceptual constructions arising from their latent impressions would have no activity toward an object beyond the range of experience; thus, this synthesis [of experience] would not be possible.
The word "and" (ca) indicates a connection with the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (equal conjunction). In what kind of [state] else?
In that which is permeated by states such as pleasure—states that arise and perish—and which is woven together;
that is, in that which is permeated by states such as pleasure and exists like the thread of a garland within. Those...

By this [statement], which asserts that those things being connected [in the present] are objects of memory, it is established— even within the doctrine of momentary cognition— that memory, produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience,
can determine an object belonging to a past time experienced through that experience, provided all consciousness is turned inward.

However, he has indicated that everything is logical when the subject (pramātṛ) exists; therefore, enough with these discourses that produce distaste in those to be instructed who possess tender hearts. Those seeking this [truth] should examine the *Pratyabhijñā*. Since the author himself has merely sketched out the reasoning here, we [shall elaborate upon it].

Those who possess intelligence should not harbor resentment toward us on the grounds that this has been only partially disclosed. However, for the sake of refuting the Mīmāṃsakas, this should be explained as follows:
those cognitions such as "I am happy" and so forth exist elsewhere, namely, in the nature of the *puryaṣṭaka*.

In the cognizer—who is permeated by states such as pleasure and exists in a form woven like warp and woof—these states clearly exist and persist, as witnessed by common worldly experience; however, they do not exist in this nature of our own, which is the essence of Śiva, a dense mass of consciousness and bliss. Thus, this Self is not always obscured by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as pleasure and so forth, but is rather composed of pure consciousness (cinmaya). When...

However, when this [Self] remains concealing its own true nature due to its innate impurity—which will be described later—then, even during states such as that of the *puryaṣṭaka*, its nature as happiness and so forth is not obstructed by those [impurities]; this has already been stated. Therefore, this [Self] is never obscured by them. "I am thin," "I am..."
The intention of one who speaks thus— "I am happy," "I am miserable"— while avoiding cognitions such as "gross" and so forth,

is that by immersing the level of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body), which is permeated by the cognition of happiness and so on, into the inward-turned state, the external world, including the body and jars, also dissolves through that connection; thus, he indeed recognizes [the Self].
One's own nature is that of Śiva; therefore, one must exert effort in every way solely for the sake of pacifying the *puryaṣṭaka*. || 4 ||
Reiterating that all other doctrines are untenable— a conclusion established by the aforementioned reasoning—
the preeminent secret Guru, who knows logic, experience, and scripture, asserts that only the reality of *spanda* is established by reason:
"Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the object of perception nor the perceiver..."
Nor does even the state of delusion exist; yet that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality.
In this context, whatever internal objects such as pain or pleasure, or external objects such as blue or yellow there may be that are to be grasped,

as well as that which grasps them— the body consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), the senses, and so forth— it can certainly be said that, when not being perceived, as in deep sleep, they do not exist at all. However, when they are indeed perceived, then...

Since even that which is being conceptualized consists of consciousness, it follows that it is indeed consciousness alone that exists. As our supreme preceptor, the venerable Utpaladeva, the knower of the secret reality, has said: "The object to be illumined is of the nature of light; for that which is not light cannot be established" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.3).
In the *Śrīmad-Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it will also be stated here:
"Because of the realization of identity with that which consists of the nature of its own cognition" (2.3).
Therefore, that which is a single mass of pure light, wherein suffering and pleasure, blue and so forth, as well as their grasper, do not exist—[that is the Self].

The reality exists. Now, one might object: "In this way, when all objects of perception (*grāhya*) and subjects of perception (*grāhaka*) are abolished, does it not follow that the reality is essentially void (*śūnyātman*)?

To this he replies: "Nor even is there the state of delusion. For where even the state of delusion—that is, the condition of being deluded or the nature of emptiness—does not exist, that too indeed does not manifest. If it manifests, then, because its very nature is manifestation, it is not [void].

There is indeed an initial manifestation, and there is never an absence of manifestation, because if that [initial manifestation] were absent, the absence of manifestation itself would be unestablished. And this will come to pass; however, that state is not inward-turned. (1.16)

In this regard, moreover, even that state of delusion— which, though of the nature of Brahman, consists essentially in a mere luminosity devoid of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose essence is sovereignty, and which the knowers of the Upanishads have understood as "Brahman is consciousness"— cannot exist without the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

Because it is insentient (*jaḍatvāt*). As it has been stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "They know that the essential nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, even though light is colored by objects, it would be like an insentient thing such as a crystal" (*Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* 1.5.11).
Thus it is said; and in the *Bhaṭṭanāyaka-stotra* as well:
"O Lord, how much fruit could this neuter Supreme Brahman bear, were it not for Your masculine power, the beautiful woman who is Your devotion?"
Thus, that very reality which has been investigated from the passage beginning with "where it is situated" (sthitam) exists;
and it exists indeed in its ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) in a form established by reasoning, experience, and scripture.
Furthermore, it exists in its ultimate, non-constructed, and perfect form, and not in a constructed manner like blue and other such objects. As it was said by the Great Teachers:
"Thus, these insentient things, which are mere mental constructs in relation to the self, exist only within the Light;
for the Light alone exists by its own nature through both itself and others. (Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 13).
Thus it was also stated by the venerable Bhartṛhari.
Whatever exists at the beginning, whatever exists at the end, and whatever exists in the middle—that alone possesses reality;
for that which does not manifest has no reality whatsoever.

Thus, because all sentences possess an exclusive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), the particle *eva* (only/alone) must be applied three times here. In this way, by means of this aphorism, [the author] refutes all those who maintain that there is a continuum of consciousness in the form of pleasure and so forth; those who maintain that the reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*) is defiled by pleasure and so forth;
those who maintain the plurality of the grasped and the grasper; and all those who maintain nihilism.
Having refuted as non-existent the doctrine of those who maintain that Brahman is a light devoid of all grasping— [the reading in manuscript *kh* is "brahmatattvavādinām"]—
it is asserted that the ultimate reality exists solely as the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*). Furthermore, in this very [reality]...

When the *spanda-tattva*—the essence of which is radiant manifestation and which is cultivated by great souls who are attentive to the oral instructions—shines forth, then this world of suffering and pleasure, the grasped and the grasper, their absence, and so forth, though existing, is nothing at all;
for the sole essence of everything is this wonder (*camatkāra*). Therefore, it has been taught that "this very thing exists. As the Great Teachers have said:
"Even sufferings become happiness, even poison becomes nectar, and even saṃsāra becomes liberation—where this is so, that is the path of Śaṅkara. (Uttara-stotra 20.12).
The path of Śaṅkara is the expansion in the form of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), which is the cause for attaining the essential nature of Śaṅkara’s own self.
Thus, for the sake of recognizing the reality that has been established through reasoning, he describes the means accompanied by higher knowledge (*abhijñā*),
because this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts as if undeluded,
performing the processes of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal along with the internal wheel. (6)
One should diligently and with reverence examine that reality through such effort,
for its independence is everywhere innate.
That reality has been determined with reverence, faith, and effort; for it is said,
"Bhairava is exertion" (Śiva Sūtra 1.5), which, by withdrawing all dualities, is established as the essence of the Śiva Sūtras.

It is to be examined by means of the exertion (*udyama*) in the form of Bhairava, which consists of the service of one's own inward-turned nature that is full through the expansion of the activity of its own vital energy (*ojas*). For this [exertion] is the unartificial, innate, and independent sovereignty (*svatantratā*)— whose essence is the principle of vibration (*spanda*)— of that very nature of Śiva, which is self-evident to everyone as "this."

The ellipsis "is situated" (*sthitā*) is to be supplied, meaning she vibrates everywhere within the domain of both the insentient and the sentient. To the question "What is that reality? he replies with the passage beginning "from which" (*yataḥ*) and ending with "obtains" (*labhate*).

The word "this" (*ayam*) refers to what is well-known in the world in the form of the physical eye-socket and so forth, and not to that which is established by scripture, because the latter is eternally beyond direct perception and thus cannot be referred to as "this."
Due to the absence of instruction, the group of instruments—the thirteen faculties—becomes especially deluded;
under the influence of *māyā*, it becomes an appearance of insentience, attaining a state of delusion even greater than that of the deluded individual soul (*aṇu*).
Like one who is not deluded and like a conscious being, it independently undergoes the processes of activity, maintenance, and withdrawal, directed toward sense objects.
The meaning is that one becomes attached there and subsequently turns away from it. How so? "Together with the intermediate wheel" (*sahāntareṇa cakreṇa*).

Here, the "intermediate wheel" refers to the mistresses of the instruments (*karaṇeśvaryo*), not the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇāni*), because those are already included by the word "group" (*varga*).
It does not refer to the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) to be described later, since the three internal organs situated therein are already accounted for by the very word "group."

Because the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), which consist of nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*), have already been grasped, they cannot be established as the actual agents of activity and so forth for the person being instructed; furthermore, since the yogi— who has directly perceived the subtle elements and is himself intent upon the contemplation of the supreme reality— cannot be the object of instruction, [the subtle elements cannot be the cause].

Therefore, this opinion of certain [authorities] is incorrect. By the phrase "the deluded one like one undeluded," only the aggregate of the instruments (*karaṇavarga*) is to be connected, and not even the internal wheel of the Mistress of the Instruments (*karaṇeśvarī-cakra*), because that consists of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*).
The intention of one who asserts this is as follows: that this very Self is Śaṅkara.

The self-nature of that which performs the most difficult feats— by its sovereignty— simultaneously manifests as a single unity both the circle of the mistresses of the senses, whose essence is consciousness, and the group of instruments, which has the form of insentient appearance;
thus it causes [them] to perform the functions of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, whereby the divine mistresses of the senses act accordingly.
In this way, they perform the creation of various states and so forth; likewise, although the group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*) is insentient, it appears as if it were an agent.

Even though, according to the secret vision (*rahasyadṛṣṭi*), there is no such thing as an insentient group of instruments, but rather the Lords of the Instruments (*karaṇeśvarī*), whose bodies are consciousness, who manifest themselves [in that form], nevertheless, here [in this teaching], one must instruct [the disciple] in accordance with well-established conventional perception.
It has been stated that one should enter into the instruction on the secret meaning by means of this sequence. And thus,
by means of the activity of the group of instruments consisting of the *golaka* (the physical body) and so forth,

one who gathers together his own circle of rays (*marīcicakra*)— which is the nature of the presiding subject— [discovers] that which impels both [the body and the senses], namely, the venerable Śaṅkara-natured [Self].
One's own true nature (svasvarūpa) must be examined, for by that very act it is also stated that upon attaining it, this yogin shall possess its unartificial sovereignty (svātantrya) everywhere.
This alone is worthy of examination because it is the supreme object to be attained, and it is precisely this that one must examine.

Because it is achievable through reasoning and because it is an easy means, one should therefore act with great respect, characterized by not obstructing the enjoyment of desired objects. Here, the time for examination has arrived, according to the instructions of this world; as it was said by the secret masters:
"May these functions of the senses, though radiant, proceed each in its own respective station;
O Lord, let there never be, even for a moment or in the slightest degree, the rashness of impairing the flavor of non-difference from You. (Upaniṣad-stotra 8).

Here, the *kṛtya* suffixes (*pratantu*) are used in the sense of what is fit to be examined, what is possible, the arrival of the proper time, or as a command. Furthermore, [the subject] is dull-witted.

By asserting that "it is witnessed by the experience of everyone that the group of instruments (the senses) obtains activity and so forth through its power as if it were not deluded," [the author] refutes the Cārvāka and others who maintain that the senses and so forth possess consciousness.
Now, how was it stated [in the previous verse]: "Then, having attained, as it were, sentience from that reality, the senses themselves engage in activity and so forth"?
The meaning is that they obtain [their objects] because this very perceiver impels the instruments, such as the hands and so forth, according to his will.

Regarding what was also said—that "that reality must be examined with effort"—he speaks out of the following apprehension: "How can this be, since our will pursues only external things and does not venture to engage in the examination of reality? Thus he says:
For this [mantra] does not function as an impeller by means of desire or instigation;
rather, through contact with its own power, the person becomes equal to it.

This worldly person does not proceed because of a mere desire acting as a push or a goad to impel his instruments toward their respective functions; rather, it is through contact with the power of his own conscious nature— which consists of the principle of *spanda*— and through even a slight immersion (*āveśa*) produced by that, he becomes equal to it.

Indeed, even that which is insentient attains sentience through the sprinkling of the drops of the essence of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā-rasa*). Therefore, that reality not only [animates] the instruments, but by animating even the subject—who was previously imagined and suspected as their impeller—it makes itself the locus of activity and so forth, whereby this conceit arises in him: "I..."

"I impel the instruments [of action]. However, even without the penetration (*anuvedha*) of the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*), it is entirely logical that one must examine that very principle which brings about the state of consciousness for both the instruments and the perceiver through the penetration by the expansion of its own circle of rays (*svaraśmicakraprasara*), based on the thought "it is nothing at all. Furthermore, if [this occurs] by means of that which is called Will (*icchā*), acting as a goad (*pratoda*):

If one instrument were to impel other instruments, then that very instrument called "will" (icchā), being itself something to be impelled, would require another instrument to impel it, and that too would require yet another; thus there would be an infinite regress.
As for what was said—that "our will does not strive to act upon that"—there too, the first [point]...
The half-verse should be understood as an admission, while the subsequent portion is to be applied as a rebuttal:

"It is true that this person cannot set desire in motion for the sake of investigating reality, nor is he able to make reality the object of desire because it is non-conceptual; rather, [it is] desire that pursues objects."

When, preceded by the enjoyment of that [object], one has pacified [the mind] and touches the inward-turned power of the Self—the principle of vibration (*spanda-tattva*)—which carries consciousness within one's own senses, then one becomes equal to That;
through absorption in That, one attains autonomy everywhere, just like That. Because it is so, therefore it is the *tattva* (the true reality).
The meaning is that it is to be examined. Because the ground of power (*śakti-bhūmi*) is characterized primarily by touch, it is said to be "from the touch of one's own strength."
Now, one might object: "Since this field is composed of the Supreme Lord, why does it not always manifest in its absolute fullness?
Why does it depend upon contact with the inward-turned power of the Self? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For one who is incapable due to innate impurity, yet desires to perform what ought to be done..."
When agitation is completely dissolved, then the supreme state is attained.

One's own, belonging to oneself, and manifested through one's own sovereignty, this power of will (*icchā-śakti*), whose nature is the non-recognition of one's true essence, becomes contracted; being of the form of the conceit of incompleteness, it is the impurity known as the *āṇava-mala*. Because of the turbidity caused by the pentad of coverings (*kañcuka*) arising from that impurity, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) [becomes obscured] in succession.

The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is indeed impurity (*aśuddhi*), which, through the prior assumption of extreme contraction by undergoing the state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the sense organs (*indriya*), as well as the states of being a limited knower (*kiṃcijjñatva*) and a divided omniscience (*bhedasarvajñatva*), takes the form of the manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge (*bhinnavedya-prathā-rūpa*), which is the *māyīya* stain. This occurs gradually.

Having first undergone the contraction of assuming the forms of the organs of action—characterized by differentiation, universal agency, and limited agency—it attains an extreme state of limitation; this impurity consisting of the performance of auspicious and inauspicious acts is the *kārmamala*. Due to that [impurity], one becomes incapable, devoid of perfect knowledge and agency, and for that very reason...

Those who desire the performance of worldly and scriptural duties, yet are constantly tormented by the non-attainment of their desired objects due to being overwhelmed by longing— supported by the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated, as well as by direct experience— they are perceivers who are rendered helpless by their own desires.

The meaning is that, preceded by the cessation of the conceit of self in what is non-self, the cessation of the conceit of non-self in the Self should attain the status of being the object of recognition; however, this does not happen at that very moment, because of its eternity. And it has been said in the *Vijñānabhairava*:
"When the fourfold— mind, volition, power, and self—
is completely exhausted in the Beloved, then that is the Bhairava-body" (verse 138).
Those who maintain that by the term "one's own impurity" there exists a separate substance called *mala* [should reflect as follows]:
They were castigated as being corruptible. || 9 ||

Now, one might raise the objection that when the agitation within the self—which consists of the sense of "I" as the subject—has subsided, it follows that reality must be motionless, like a waveless ocean; he dispels this doubt by stating:
"Then its innate nature, characterized by consciousness and agency, [remains]."
For he knows all that is desired and brings it about. || 10 ||

The word "then" (*tadā*) refers to the perspective of the disciple; it denotes the uncreated, innate nature (*sahaja-dharma*), which is the essential being (*svabhāva*) of the Supreme Lord characterized by the previously mentioned autonomy.
This consists of knowledge and action—whose essence is light and bliss existing in a state of equilibrium—which constitute the defining characteristic, that is, the infallible nature, of [the Lord].

The meaning is that when the agitation of this person has subsided, such [knowledge] becomes manifest for him. From what does this become manifest? He says: because at that time, upon entering the supreme state (*paramapada*), whatever was desired—whatever he had sought to know or intended to do—during his desire to enter, all that he knows and performs.

The two *ca*s here express simultaneity, but not in the manner that some claim the two *ca*s indicate the identity of cognition and action; for that [identity] has already been established by the very mention of the related term characterized as "the nature of being a knower and an agent."
This was stated by one who expresses the actual nature of reality. || 10 ||

Now, for one who— by means of firm reliance on the *spanda-tattva* (the reality of vibration), which is directly realized through the stabilization of the process of unfolding (*unmeṣa*) as set forth in the aphorism "Now, from the instrument" (*atha yataḥ karaṇa*) and "one's own impurity" (*nijāśuddhi*)—
makes even the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) of a single flavor with meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there occurs the severance of worldly existence (*bhava*).
He says that this occurs for one who, observing that very nature as the presiding agent, remains as if smiling; for such a person, whence could this crooked path arise? (11)

Observing and investigating that innate nature of his own, which consists of the principle of *spanda*, as being recognized through the aforementioned logical proofs and perceptions, and which pervades him even during the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*) by way of its presiding presence; he reflects upon it.
"Power, in the form of the vital breath (*marut*), should neither go out nor enter when [the aperture] is expanded;
by means of that [power], through a state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*), one assumes the form of Bhairava in the center. (Viṣṇubhairavakalpa 26).
Thus it is said.

Having simultaneously cast all powers— beginning with vision— toward their respective objects of knowledge in every direction by means of the mind, You remain in the center like a pillar of gold, appearing as the one who possesses the form of the universe.
Thus, by means of the logic of the tradition as indicated in the *Śrīvijñānabhairavakakṣyāstotra*,
through the samādhi of closing and opening [the eyes],
and by taking hold of the pervasive middle ground simultaneously, one ascends the two friction-sticks (*araṇi*) of emission (*visarga*).
With the inner object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening the eyes—
this is that Bhairavī Mudrā, hidden in all the Tantras.
Thus, having entered the mudrā of Bhairava as taught in the tradition,
he beholds the vast multitude of objective phenomena— which, like a collection of various reflections sinking and emerging within a mirror—
though arisen in the very space of consciousness, dissolves back into that same space.

Through the recognition of his own true nature— which is supramundane, a mass of supreme bliss unprecedented throughout thousands of births— all mental fluctuations are instantly severed; smiling as if having entered the seal of wonder,
and by attaining a great expansion, he suddenly realizes his own appropriate and authentic essential being.

The meaning is this: for that lord of yogis who remains established and does not become slackened due to any support, this—referring to the wretched course of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) which causes the entire world to tremble and consists of the continuous succession of birth, death, and so forth—how could it arise? It certainly does not, because of the absence of its cause, namely one's own impurity. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*,
it is stated that one whose mind is unwavering in reality (*tattva*), even while enjoying sense objects,
is not touched by defects at all, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.

"Just as one who is equipped with mantras and other means that remove poison does not lose consciousness even while consuming poison, so too is the yogi of great intelligence. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 18.120).

Now, in order to awaken those such as the followers of the Upaniṣads, Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas), and the Mādhyamikas— who teach that at the dissolution of the cosmic agitation, only a reality consisting of non-existence remains in the form of the total destruction of the universe— the author demonstrates the supramundane nature of the body of this treatise by means of an antidote to the reality accepted by them.
He explains the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*): Non-existence does not become an object of contemplation, nor is there a state of non-delusion therein;
for, through contact with diligent practice, the certainty arises that "it existed. (12)
Therefore, that [state] should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep;
for such a state of being remembered does not truly attain the nature of reality.

By such statements as "Non-being alone was this in the beginning" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), the non-existence favored by the knowers of other Vedāntic schools cannot be an object of meditative cultivation (*bhāvyatā*).

This is because meditation has as its object a thing that is to be cultivated (*bhāvya-vastu*), whereas non-existence is nothing at all; or, if it were to become something through being cultivated, it would cease to be non-existence.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of the state of being real, how can that which is the absence even of the one who contemplates (the emptiness) be contemplated as the destruction of the universe? For if the contemplator is admitted, then there is no destruction of the universe, because the contemplator remains; thus, the non-existence of the universe itself is not the reality. Now, suppose this [destruction] is merely imagined.

The position is that the practitioner, meditating upon the universal negation (viśvoccheda) as it is conceptually constructed, becomes non-existent in nature at the completion of that meditation due to identity with the object of meditation. To this, it is replied:
in that meditation on non-existence, there is no absence of delusion; nor is there any lack of delusion therein, but rather, there is only delusion.
Upon the completion of cultivation, that result of conceptual cognition becomes clear.
According to this principle, if non-existence—which consists in the annihilation of the entire universe—is cultivated, the attainment of the ultimate truth will never occur.
Now, it might be argued:
"By means of all objects of cognition and all phenomena, and by all principles without exception..."
It is empty of all latent tendencies of the afflictions, yet it is not empty from the perspective of ultimate reality.

Thus it was said by Nāgārjuna: "That is empty. This is true, provided that the ultimate ground—which is a mass of consciousness-bliss, autonomous, and serves as the foundational wall—is accepted, as is taught in the *Vijñānabhairava* and other scriptures concerning the Supreme Goddess.

By the passage beginning with "Transcending the measurement of space and time" (Viśvabhairava-tantra 14), the ultimate ground of consciousness (*cidbhūmi*), which serves as the foundational wall, is established; therein, the meditation on the void (*śūnyabhāvanā*) is taught.
Otherwise, this statement "it is not the void" would be a mere void itself, because it has been demonstrated that "if this were spoken, it would be excessive."
That certain state which is said to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and is unknowable by those like me is not, however,
merely a worldly convention that conforms to the meaning of nihilism.

Thus it is stated in the *Ālokamālā*. That [statement] is true; however, let it be said that what is unknowable to those like you is "unknowable," but from where does the term "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) come? For as long as even emptiness is cultivated, it must be distinguished by the wise, because it is delineated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And if that [emptiness] were for those like you...

It is impossible to know [the truth] through one's own whimsical conduct; rather, one must perform service to a true guru who is proficient in the direct realization of those respective stages, and not [merely practice] emptiness. Otherwise, both oneself and others would be cast into a bottomless, great delusion—enough said! Now, from what is it known that there is delusion in that regard? To this, he provides the answer with the words "since" (*yataḥ*).

An inquiry (*abhiyoga*) is the nature of a reflective deliberation directed toward a particular state—such as "What was I like when I arose from my absorption?"—and the verbal expression thereof. Because of contact with that [deliberation], and by virtue of it as the cause, there arises the certainty: "I was then in such a state. Since there is the realization, "I was profoundly deluded," therefore that state is indeed one of delusion (*moha*).

Since it is imagined and likewise remembered, and since it is being experienced, it rather makes known the existence of the experiencing knower (pramātṛ) whose nature is that of the abiding subject; it does not, however, indicate non-existence.
Thus, even in the state where the universe is absent, the undivided form of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) remains intact.

It has been stated that the non-existence of that [object] can never be asserted. Now, one might object: "Blue and so forth, which have been perceived, are remembered with certainty; however, there is no certainty regarding that which has become void and whose cognitive activity has subsided.

Therefore, how can it be said that 'it existed then,' since that statement is based on a certainty arising at a later time? That [later cognition] is merely a state of delusion. To this, it is replied:

This is the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*): as long as it has not been determined by the subject (*pramātṛ*) through its own self-ascension—that is, by identifying that "this-ness" with "this-ness"—it cannot be remembered. The knower (*vedaka*), however, even when contracted in states such as the imagined void (*śūnya*), remains the ultimate reality of non-conventional *ahantā*; thus, there is no separateness for him within his own self.

The conceptual construction that determines this is itself "I," which is then established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as the very nature of the void subject; and because it is the correlate of the universe, it possesses contraction as its essence and is subsequently remembered. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, for it is therefore of the nature of that void.
Therefore, by that very principle stated [in the verse]: "Whatever is spoken excessively, whether it be real or unreal, is artificial.
Thus, according to that logic...

The meaning is that it was brought forth by the Supreme Lord Himself through the cultivation of the unreal (*abhūtabhāvanā*) for the sake of concealing His knowledge, and thus manifested as an object of attainment for the deluded. "That which is to be known" (*jñeya*) means that which is to be cognized, and its nature is such that it is always like deep sleep; this is the illustration. The underlying idea is that it is always like a state of deep sleep.

Delusion itself is established without effort and exists for everyone; so what need is there for this other void acquired through the exertion of meditative concentration, since there is no difference between the two in their lack of reality? Moreover, this void is a great ocean of delusion that is difficult to cross.

In this way, many who are primarily adherents of Vedānta, Akṣapāda (Nyāya), Sāṃkhya, Sugata (Buddhism), and so forth, have entered [this path]. Furthermore, for those seeking to enter the reality of Spanda whose efforts have become slackened, this void is an obstacle. As he will say:
Then, beginning with the words "in that great void" (1.25),
[the text describes] the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*), which is deluded...

Thus, it is evident that the author exhibits great zeal toward its eradication. Accordingly, although this has already been determined here as something to be abandoned, it will be determined once again as an effort directed toward the goal. * * * * * * * * ##?

Regarding this point: since we have undertaken this refutation for that reason, Your Honors should not feel any anger toward us while lending an ear to our instructions. For once the Buddhists have been refuted, those who maintain the doctrines of the Upaniṣads (Śrutyantavādins) and others are likewise refuted by the same logic.
Nothing more has been said. Now we shall speak of that which is the subject at hand: this principle called *spanda*.

It does not become something unremembered like the void (*śūnya*), because it is impossible for that which is always of a single nature as the continuous perceiver to ever be non-perceived. And so they have said:
"By what means could one know the Knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

And although the state of immersion is remembered by one who has emerged from it due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the vital breaths and so forth, nevertheless, the reality of vibration (*spandatattva*) is not merely that much.
That [reality] is indeed the nature of the supreme subject, whose essence is light and bliss, all-pervasive and uninterrupted.
As he will say:
"Therefore, among the reflections upon words and their meanings, there is no state that is not Śiva" (2.4).

Thus, for this [consciousness], whose nature is uninterrupted aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), there can never be the state of being remembered or the state of being deluded (*mūḍhatva*). As for the fact that it is referred to here by the word "that" (*tat*) as "that reality" (*tattvam*), that is because its own self is not liberated from its sovereignty (*svātantrya*).

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā Kārikā*, [this applies] only to that which is imagined and lacks an ultimate nature, but not to that which is real in the absolute sense. By the phrase "it is not apprehended," he means this: there is no cognition whatsoever of this reality by way of being remembered. 13.

Now, one might raise the following objection: "In passages such as *nanu yatra sthitam*, it was stated that the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) assumes the form of all cosmic effects (*viśvakārya*).

Since that assumed form is produced by meditation (*dhyāna*), artificial (*kṛtrima*), and non-existent (*abhāvātmaka*), how can this [consciousness] possess the state of being uninfatuated (*amūḍhatva*), which consists of uninterrupted aesthetic wonder (*anavacchinnacamatkāra*)? To address this doubt, he says:
And here, there are two states designated as "being an effect" and "being an agent.
Among these, being an effect is perishable, whereas agency is imperishable. (14)
Only that effort which is directed toward external objects is lost here;
when that is lost, the ignorant person thinks, "I am destroyed," yet he does not perceive that inward-turned state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience.
Its disappearance might sometimes occur because of the non-perception of anything else. (16)

In this *spandatattva*, there exists a pair of states designated as "objectivity" (*kāryatva*) and "agency" (*kartṛtva*), which are differentiated merely by verbal convention; for in reality, it is that single reality alone—
the nature of Śiva, who is autonomous light— that [exists] inseparable from the being of the agent.

That which is pervaded by the activity whose nature is light, and which manifests as non-different from that [light], is called an "effect" (kārya) because it assumes forms such as non-existence while being like the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), and bodies; for nothing else besides this can logically possess causality. As it has been stated in the venerable *Abhijñā*:
"But for the insentient, there is no such power of existence that [could transform] the non-existent into the existent;
therefore, the relationship of cause and effect consists precisely in the nature of agent and object" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 2.4.2). And its being an effect is precisely this: that it...

Through the process of joining and separating the appearances of diverse places, times, and so forth, [the Light] manifests infinite appearances— such as bodies, blue objects, and the like— which, though not distinct from the very nature of the conscious Self (cidātman), appear as if distinct, like reflections in a mirror, for as long as anything at all is manifested.
