All of that, by virtue of being manifested through an outward-turned form, is subject to decay;
and its decay consists in its immersion into the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) and its subsistence in the form of "I-ness" (ahantā).
For this very reason, it is only that objective portion of the grasper—such as the body and so forth—that is created and withdrawn by the Lord. It is not [the subjective core] that is so treated.

The nature of the agent consists of the manifestation of "I-ness" and "thou-ness"; yet, even when it enters into the body and other such forms, it remains solely of the nature of the Lord. Therefore, between those two—being the object and being the agent—the state of being an object is perishable, whereas agency, which is the nature of the freedom of consciousness, is imperishable, even amidst the arising and passing away of the universe.
Because it does not deviate from its own nature; for if it were to deviate, neither the arising nor the passing away of the world would even manifest.
Thus, even in states such as delusion, this [consciousness] remains undeluded, its essence being the unbroken wonder [of self-luminosity].
Now, one might object: "We do not perceive its agency during deep sleep and similar states, when the accomplishment of the meditative absorption on non-existence occurs."

Because no activity whatsoever is observed [therein]. It is true that the effort (*prayatna*), which consists of the impulse directed toward an effect and is inclined toward the operation of impelling the senses and so forth—that *saṃrambha*—is here, at the stage where effects have ceased, dissolved and cut off; and when that has been dissolved...

The ignorant one, whose true nature has been stolen away by the meditative absorption on non-existence (*abhāva-samādhi*), being deluded, thinks, "I am lost. On the other hand, that inward-turned nature, which consists of the light of the "I" (*ahaṃtā-prakāśa-rūpa*), is for this very reason the locus of the quality of omniscience; and since this is also an indicator of [qualities] such as omnipotence, its loss can never occur. Thus it is not [the case that it is lost].
It can never be conceived that anyone else could perceive its cessation, because no such person is ever perceived;

if such a person were perceived, he would himself be that inward-turned form of consciousness. If he is not perceived, then how can there be any certainty that this state of cessation exists? Furthermore, it is not that some other person does not perceive its cessation, but rather that [the one who perceives it] is that very same [consciousness].
Since its nature is luminosity, how could there be its non-existence? Thus, in the phrase "due to the non-perception of another," the meaning is "due to the absence of perception by another agent.
Furthermore, just as the absence of a jar is ascertained through the perception of the ground or other objects as distinct from the jar;
In the same way, the non-existence of the self would also be determined by the perception of something distinct from the self;
since the existence of that which perceives it is necessarily present, the non-existence of that perceiving self is not established.
Furthermore, if that [self] were to perish upon the cessation of the effort directed toward an effect, then at a later time, for another...

The meaning is that there would be no perception of anything at all, which would entail the non-existence of the perception of other things. Furthermore, since the outward-directed effort of another [subject] is not perceived during states such as deep sleep, how can the ignorant suspect the loss of the inward-turned reality? For when one thing is lost, what has happened to the other? Moreover, of the other...

Because the effort directed toward an object is not perceived, and because this non-perception is itself manifested, there is never a cessation of that perceiver who is inward-turned and whose nature is light;
for that inward-turned state is the locus of the quality of omniscience, even during that state of apparent non-existence.

"He surely knows," for otherwise that very [agency] would not be established. In the phrase "of another" (*anyasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of both the agent (*kartari*) and the object (*karmaṇi*). It was stated that, for one who is inward-turned (*antarmukhe*), the state of being an agent is like the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) to the state of being an effect;

however, in reality, according to the reasoning already explained, he is precisely the sustainer of that state (*avasthātṛtva*). "Inward-turned" (*antarmukha*) means [turned toward] the internal, which consists of the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*).
It should be construed as: "that of which the mouth is the principal part. || 16 ||

Having thus demonstrated that the unawakened person determines the non-existence of the self as the subject— even though such non-existence is logically untenable— upon the cessation of outward-directed activity,
he now describes the nature of the perception of the self for both the well-awakened and the unawakened.
The perception of that [reality] is constant and never deviates from the three states for one who is perfectly awakened; however, for the Supreme, it exists eternally at the beginning and the end.
The perception of that fundamental nature— which is uninterrupted luminosity— is,

by virtue of the reasoning already stated, constant "always" (nityam) at the beginning, middle, and end, throughout all three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, for one who is perfectly awakened and devoid even of the latent impressions of non-awakening.

The meaning is that it is non-deviant and non-perishing; it indeed always exists, manifesting as the very nature of Śaṅkara himself. However, for another who is unawakened, when each of those ten states—which consist of their own appropriate forms of consciousness—first desires to emerge and at the end [of that process],...
This refers to the state of inwardness consisting of rest, and not to the intermediate state (*madhyapada*) which consists in the persistence of the manifestation of objects appropriate to oneself.
As it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"As long as there are states of contact with all-knowing subjects and non-knowers..."
"She is perceived as remaining [there], or rather, through rest in that, in the fruit" (*Śivasūtravimarśinī* 2.5).
Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa also explained it exactly thus in his own commentary: "at its beginning and end.
Following the words of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa’s commentary, we too, in accordance with those words of his commentary...

Untrained in explaining the meaning of the Sūtra, though it is exceedingly pure, through afflicted conceptualization, they claim that because the perception of that [state] exists at the beginning and end of one who is not well-awakened (*asuprabuddha*), for that very reason this person here is made well-awakened by the instructions on *spanda*. As he will say:
Therefore, one should be constantly diligent in discerning the reality of vibration (*spandatattva*),
whether waking, dreaming, or otherwise—
as it has been taught.
"As one who is awakened becomes unobscured, like the state of deep sleep," so it is also in the dream state. [1.25; 3.2]
"One should always remain awakened," and so forth; and also, "In these three states, beginning with waking," and so on. For here, in the three stages beginning with waking—

Just as the initial and final limits [of a word], the middle portion of the word—which consists of the determination of meaning—is also to be made to consist of the expansion of the Fourth State (*turyābhoga*); for this purpose, instruction is set forth for the sake of bringing about the state of being "well-awakened" (*suprabuddha*) in one who is already awakened.
We shall establish this point further on. And so it is stated in the *Śivasūtra*:
"In the distinction between waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there arises the expansion of the Fourth" (Śivasūtra 1.7).
Likewise, "the Fourth should be poured into the three like oil" (Śivasūtra 3.20).
Thus, the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśa) is the enjoyer of the triad. (Śiva-sūtra 1.11). || 17 ||
He demonstrates, by way of analysis, the kind of perception that occurs for one who is well-awakened regarding the three stages:

"Endowed with the supreme power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the All-pervasive Lord shines in two stages; but in the other [the third], He consists of pure consciousness. (18)

For one who is perfectly awakened, the pervasive Lord whose nature is Śaṅkara shines in the two states of waking and dreaming as His own essential nature, joined with the Supreme Power (parā-śakti) which consists of the principle of Spanda; this power, in its abundance, takes the form of knowledge and the object of knowledge in the middle state (the dreamless sleep), while in the two extremes—the beginning and end of that knowledge—it shines as His very own nature. For therein:

He perceives the entire universe as being like his own limbs, just as Sadāśiva and Īśvara do; however, this is not the case in deep sleep (*suṣupta*) as it is for others in both deep sleep and the fourth state (*turya*). Since the discussion began with the phrase "the three states are non-deviating," and because the fourth state has not yet been introduced, and because the perception [of the universe] itself constitutes the nature of the fourth state, this all-pervasive Lord appears to him as consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*).

The phrase "due to the cessation of all objects of knowledge" (*aśeṣavedyopaśamāt*) refers exclusively to the perspective of one who is perfectly awakened (*suprabuddha*), and not according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*).
Otherwise, the statement that [the self] is "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*) would become untenable;
for in the world, the state of deep sleep is characterized by delusion (*moha*), whereas from the perspective of Śiva, even the waking and dreaming states are composed of consciousness.

And even so, because it is not applicable to the present context; from this point until the end of the first *niṣyanda*, the text stands as a means for the fully awakened to attain supreme awakening (*suprabuddhatā*). Just as it was not noticed by the commentators, let it be examined by oneself;
how much shall we write for every single step? || 18 ||
He demonstrates how even these states of waking and so forth do not obstruct one who is awakened:

"The outpourings of the vibration of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth, by virtue of their reliance on the universal vibration, constantly attain their own existence and become non-obstructive to the Knower. (19)
Those for whom the principles of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* constitute the principle of *prakṛti*—
the ground of manifestation— are intended here as those abiding in the principle of *māyā*. As it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra* in the section on the arrangement of the *māyā-masūra-kas*:
"One should contemplate the covering below as red and the one above as white;
in the middle, one should know darkness (tamas). These qualities (guṇas) are thus established" (Svacchandatantra 2.65).
Of those [qualities], they are the first of the specific expansions of the movements (spanda), beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*.

Their outflows— the expansions of the body, the instruments [of perception], and the worlds, as well as cognitions such as blue or pleasure, and likewise the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth according to their respective capacities— constantly do not act as obstacles for a certain highly awakened knower who is in his final birth; they do not obscure his own true nature.

The meaning is this: since those certainties (niścaya) have obtained their self-nature through the perspective determined in the statement "resting where it relies on a form free from common vibration," they have therefore arisen from that very source and are identical with it.
To explain further:
"Regarding the entities that are the forms of His own body, the knowledge and action of the Lord—
these two, with Māyā as the third, constitute the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*).
According to this view stated in the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā*, the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) alone belongs to the Supreme Lord.
Having manifested as the triad of powers— knowledge, action, and illusion— at the level of Śrī Sadāśiva and others,
he assumes a body of play (*krīḍā-śarīra*) consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* due to the intensification of contraction; for,
because it consists of the expansion of his own power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), he is ever perfectly awakened (*suprabuddha*), knowing everything that is presided over by that very [power].
Even while not severing the fluctuations of specific qualities and so forth, one is indeed permeated by the immersion into the reality of Spanda.
He explains how these [afflictions] bind those who are unawakened:
"But these, striving to conceal the state of abiding in one's own nature, cast those of unawakened intellect onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. (20)
Generally, those of unawakened intellect— whose own *spanda*-reality, consisting of the power of the Supreme Lord, remains unrecognized, and who identify the body as the self—
are intent on obscuring their own state, which is the essence of *spanda*, by means of the outpourings of the vibrations of the qualities (*guṇas*) and so forth.
Those whose sole essence is constant exertion [toward liberation] are led across this [ocean] with great difficulty by their teachers;
thus, they cause [beings] to fall upon the path of transmigration—which is difficult to traverse, impossible to leap over, terrible, and full of suffering.
As it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"Then, having embraced the subtle *rudra*-atoms, those others are known as the most terrible powers (*aparā*) who cause those [souls] merged in sense-objects to fall. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.31).
For it is thus that this supreme power (*parāśakti*), whose essence is the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*), was previously established.

She alone is the power Vāmeśvarī, because she emits (*vamana*) both the internal and external universe and because she is the conduct of the left (*vāmācāra*) within transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
The four circles of deities (*devatā-cakra*)— namely Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī— which are raised up by her,
move upon the supreme plane for those who are well-awakened, but for those who are unawakened...
They are the impellers toward the progressively lower paths; for indeed, those very Khecarīs who move in the void of consciousness (*bodhagagana*) of the well-awakened one—
possessing [the powers of] being unconditioned by time, non-duality, universal agency, omniscience, fullness, and pervasiveness— [are they].
Existing in the form of a veil (*kañcuka*),
they are the causes of the limitations of being subject to time, limited agency, limited knowledge, attachment, and necessity;
they are the "movements" (*gocaryaḥ*) that range within the domains of intellect, ego, and mind, which consist of discursive thought and are characterized by that [veiling].
For the well-awakened, they produce determination, conceit, and volition consisting of non-difference from one's own Self;

for the deluded, however, they produce those whose sole essence is duality. Moving within the ten directions, which are the domains of the external senses, these "direction-movers" (dikcaryas) consist of the expansion of non-duality for the well-awakened, while for others, they are the causes of the expansion of duality. Earth.

The fivefold objects of knowledge, consisting of form and the rest, are the "ground-dwellers" (*bhūcarīs*) moving therein; by becoming solidified through the state of being absorbed in that [object], they attain identity with it. These ground-dwellers manifest themselves as the body of the light of consciousness for the well-awakened one, while for others, they appear entirely limited.

Existing as "expanding," these four wheels— which consist of the vibration (*spanda*) of the *guṇas* and so forth— cast both worldly people of unawakened intellect, who exist in the form of the knower, the internal and external organs, and the objects of knowledge,

and likewise yogins who are satisfied merely with the expansion of *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, into the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), which consists of the unfolding of those respective principles (*tattva*).
Therefore,
one who is constantly engaged in the discernment of the reality of vibration (spandatattva) attains his own true nature even while awake before long. || 21 ||

One who is constantly striving for the discernment— that is, the contemplative realization— of the *spanda-tattva* (the principle of vibration) whose nature has been described and will be further described;

who, according to the perspective stated in the *Bhagavad Gītā* (12.2), "Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me, ever-disciplined," is perpetually intent upon contemplating his own inward-turned nature while still in the waking state.

Remaining precisely in the state of wakefulness, one attains in no time one's own innate nature, which consists of Śaṅkara; thus, his inner nature, whose essence is Śaṅkara, emerges by itself, whereby the awakened one becomes "well-awakened" through the attainment of the ever-arisen immersion (*samāveśa*).
The meaning is that he becomes liberated while living. || 21 ||

These are those fixed states in which, for one thus exerted, the cessation of vibration— consisting in the effortless destruction of all other mental fluctuations arising through the power of a strong object— is unveiled and becomes manifest.
To teach that these are the objects of initial exertion, the Teacher says:
"Whether one is extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or when deliberating 'What shall I do?', or while running—whatever state one reaches, therein movement is established. (22)
In all cases, on the path of means (*upāyamārga*), yogins first pacify all other mental fluctuations and then become one-pointed;
even in these states such as extreme anger, which consist of the cessation of all other fluctuations by their very nature,
if one is constantly striving for the discernment of the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*).

Yogins instantly become inward-turned and attain their desired goal without delay; however, the point is that non-yogins are merely deluded in this regard. For instance, upon seeing an enemy who has just inflicted a cruel injury, or hearing words that strike at one's vital points—
At the very first moment, by the power of the deity of the desire to withdraw [the world] which is just beginning to manifest, the circle of rays turns inward;
at that same instant, by the force of the deity of full desire which is emerging, all the senses expand and rush forward.
Then, reflecting and conceptualizing "I shall do it," one enters into a state characterized by the ascent of a stream of doubt.

With all objective supports exhausted, with the expansion of his mental fluctuations rendered supportless by the blossoming consciousness of doubt, he flees with extreme haste— like one pursued by a mad elephant and the like— running regardless of his body, impelled by the goddess of effort who has directed the expansion of his other mental fluctuations toward his own self.

In states such as those produced by the great terror of beholding a lion or a python, when a yogin who is constantly striving for the discernment of the reality of *spanda* reaches and abides in that state consisting of the cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-kṣaya*), then *spanda* is established within him in that particular state characterized by the cessation of fluctuations.
The reality of vibration (spandatattva) remains ever present before one. Therefore, having recognized this state of the cessation of mental fluctuations,
one should immediately— by the method of contracting the limbs like a tortoise— subside the fluctuations of anger and doubt,
or else by the method of pervasive great expansion.
The yogi should cultivate the awareness of his own inherent power of vibration as it manifests, expanding the movements of intense joy and running; as it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:
"Within the sphere of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy..."

"Having made the intellect motionless, that reality alone remains. (Vijñānabhairava 10.1) "When great bliss is attained, or when a long-lost kinsman is seen, one should meditate upon the arising bliss and become absorbed in it, with the mind fixed on that alone. (Vijñānabhairava 71)

"In hunger and other [afflictions], in fear, in grief, in the deep forest, in flight from an elephant, in curiosity, and at the end of hunger and other [states], the reality of Brahman is near. (Viśvabhārati Bhairavī 11.8) || 22 ||

Thus, having first cultivated the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) in these states through the stated reasoning, and subsequently maintaining that very awareness in all states, one who is constantly diligent should attain the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which consists in entering into the firmness of that [power].
He remains having formed the resolve: "I shall certainly do whatever he will say, relying upon that state which he shall teach. (23)
Relying upon that [channel], both the Moon and the Sun set on the upward path along the way of the Suṣumṇā,
leaving behind the domain of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved,
one who was previously deluded becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep.

This is the nature of my self as Śaṅkara: whatever he shall speak—namely, that previously experienced essential nature which is a mass of consciousness and bliss, once made manifest—he will cause me to reflect upon it; therefore, having abandoned outward-directedness, I shall certainly do it.

Having formed the resolve and reached the certainty, "I shall indeed become inclined toward that," one should take hold of that state which consists of vibration, is a mass of consciousness and bliss, and has been previously experienced even in states such as extreme anger.

The yogi who, intending [that state] as the goal to be attained, abides in and partakes of that non-conceptual state in which the movement of conceptualization has been stilled, by virtue of being unwavering—
relying upon that state of his, both the moon and the sun, namely the apāna and the prāṇa, [are restrained].
Having met in the ground of the heart, they set out simultaneously through the path of the *suṣumnā*,
the channel of Brahman, by way of the upward course of the *udāna* breath; how do they, as they subside,
abandon their objective range characterized by the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)?

Having abandoned the *maṇḍala* presided over by Brahmā, who is the presiding deity of the *brahmabila*, and having relinquished the pervasion of the body up to the upper lid [of the cranial aperture], one then reaches that Great Space (*mahāvyoma*) wherein the moon and sun— described above as being thoroughly dissolved (*prakarṣeṇa līnau*)— have transcended the pervasion of the body.

Even when the supreme space (paramākāśa), which consists of the complete cessation of all objects of knowledge, has been attained, one who—due to slackened effort—is deluded by the outflow of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth through the states of *khecarī* and the rest, becomes like the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*).
By "deep sleep," both the state of dreaming and the state of sound sleep are indicated; thus, it is like the states of dreaming and deep sleep.
The yogi who dwells only upon stages such as emptiness (*śūnya*) is said to be deluded, for his own true nature remains correctly unmanifested. As stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa:
"Relying upon that state whose essence is vibration (*spanda*)."
Thus say the yogins;
and thus,
for one whose manifestation of their own true nature has not properly occurred, [it occurs] through dreams and so forth.
"One who is deluded and unawakened would be obstructed.

However, he who, even in that state, does not slacken for even a moment due to the strength of his effort and the power of his exertion, is said to be "awakened" because he remains established solely as the nature of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), being unsubdued by darkness (*tamas*). For this very reason:
"A yogi must indeed be one who exerts constant effort"—thus has it been instructed by the Gurus. May there be auspiciousness! || 25 ||
Thus ends the first outflow, "The Vibration of One's Own Nature," in the *Spandanirṇaya* composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Kṣemarāja Anaka. 1.

Now follows the second outflow (*niṣyanda*). Thus, having established through the first outflow the *spandatattva*— which consists of its own essential nature, is supported by reasoning, is accompanied by the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and is to be recognized through the re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the closing-concentration (*nimīlanasamādhi*)— [the author explains] how it is constant...
By the attainment of that essential nature, the state of perfect awakening has been previously indicated; likewise, now,
in order to determine through reasoning the universal selfhood (*vaiśvātmya*) of that very [nature]— which is to be recognized through the unfolding of the samādhi—
I shall present this second *niṣyanda* (outflow), called the "Arising of Innate Knowledge" (*sahajavidyodaya*), which reveals the non-difference from consciousness everywhere.

He explains this with seven verses beginning with "tadākramya" and ending with "śivasadbhāvadāyinī. In that context, the universe is twofold, distinguished as pure and impure. Among these, the pure—consisting of mantras and so forth—is born from that [pure source], is composed of that, and rests within that; this has been stated in two verses. The impure is also...

"That it is indeed composed of that" is stated by the following two verses; "one who has ascended to the realization of that is liberated while living" is stated by [the next] verse; and "by the attainment of this very reality alone, practitioners achieve their own desired goal" is stated by two verses—this is the summary. Now, the text is being explained.
Regarding what was stated:
"All this effect resides here and has emerged from it" (1.2),
therein, first, that which is pure in the form of mantra and so forth is indeed produced from that very source and by its power alone.
Shining forth, it rests right there;
preceded by examples constructed from its first outpouring, he defines it:
"Having seized that power, the mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One."
They proceed toward their respective domains, like the sense organs of embodied beings. || 1 ||
Right there they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless; together with the mind of the worshipper, these possess the nature of Śiva. || 2 ||
Having seized— that is, having firmly taken as their non-dual support— the power consisting of the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*), which is the vital force (*prāṇa*) and vigor (*vīrya*),

the venerable mantras, beginning with Ananta, Vyomavyāpin, and others, exulting and expanding through the power of omniscience— the capacity for omniscience and so forth— for the sake of the spiritual authority of embodied beings.
The meaning is that they proceed by performing creation, dissolution, concealment, grace, and so forth. The word "omniscient" (sarvajña) emphasizes the state of being;

it implies omnipotence and other such qualities. Just as the instruments of embodied beings proceed toward the illumination of objects and other functions by taking hold of their power through the perspective already established, [so too does the Lord].

The illustration: likewise, those who are stainless—having accomplished their task and whose impurities of office have ceased, whose essential nature as the Self is the peaceful and distinguished denoter—merge perfectly and pre-eminently, through non-differentiation, into that very power consisting of vibration; they are liberated from the impurities of office by means of the mind of the worshipper, never to return.
Together with the perception of the world of lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), as it has been said:
"Having taken hold of the multitude of atoms as described, they have gone to the state free from affliction" (*Mālinīvijayottara* 1.41).
And because they have arisen from that very source and are emitted by its power, they dissolve back into that same place; therefore, these...

The meaning is that those [beings] such as the Mantras and Mantreśvaras possess a nature (dharma) or essence (svabhāva) belonging to Śiva, the Supreme Lord; they are thus characterized by having the general vibration (sāmānyaspanda) as their core. Now, since the emergence and so forth of the instruments (karaṇas) and the Mantras occur equally from that [source], why is it that the instruments do not possess forms such as omniscience and the rest?
It is said that the Supreme Lord, by means of his power of *māyā*, fashions bodies and instruments composed of duality;

however, by means of his power of *vidyā*, he [fashions] mantras whose bodies consist of the various reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) of denotators belonging to the sphere of space. Even in the state of *māyā*, there exists a denotator.
"According to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: 'This determination that "this is a jar" is the power of the Supreme Lord, which shines like the Self itself, transcending name and form,
and not as a mere "this-ness" (idantā),' [the cognition] does not transcend the level of the subject (*pramātṛ*)."

Since these [impurities] possess the capacity to contract consciousness— just like the body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth— it is entirely logical that they [the individual souls] lack omniscience and other such qualities.
And this [contraction] occurs when difference appears as a single, uniform essence...

Thus it has been shown by Vitasta in the *Śrīpratyabhijñākārikāṭīkā*. In this way, this should be explained with reference to the infinite lords (bhaṭṭāraka) such as Ananta, who reside in the state of the level of knowledge (*vidyāpada*) and perform the effects of emanation and so forth.
Likewise, for all [entities] in the form of instruments belonging to the teachers (*ācārya*) and others engaged in initiation and the like.
The mantras, having seized the power that consists of the reality of their own vibration and having firmly grasped it as the vitalizing principle,

proceed toward the very same [state] for the sake of the entitlement to the means of liberation, enjoyment, and so forth, together with the mind of the worshipper belonging specifically to the teacher and others.

Having bodies whose nature consists of words that express tranquility, they are therefore stainless (*nirañjana*) and pure, and they dissolve completely—that is, they come to rest. In this interpretation, the phrase "together with the mind of the worshipper" is to be connected with the preceding verse. And thus, although the activity of mantras pervades both the poles of emergence and dissolution, it remains their foundational support (*bhittibhūta*).

Thus it has been stated: in this way, it is declared that within the Śaiva tradition—which is divided into ten, eighteen, and other such categories—the very essence of the mantras is the principle of Spanda (vibration). || 2 ||

Having thus established that the creation conceived as pure— consisting of the forms of mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth— is the very nature of Śiva, he now demonstrates that even that creation conceived as impure, consisting of the forms of Māyā and so forth, is indeed the essential nature of Śiva; in doing so,
he also introduces the perspective of the secret teachings of the *Śrīmata* and other scriptures.
Because the individual soul consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being, by virtue of its nature as the consciousness thereof and through the realization of identity with it. (3)
Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva;
the enjoyer alone always abides everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment.

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is the perceiver, consisting of all things, and possesses a universal form like Śiva— for that reason, among words as denoters, meanings as the denoted, and thoughts in the form of conceptual cognition and so forth,
there is no state whatsoever— whether in the beginning, middle, or end— that is not Śiva; indeed, everything is [Śiva].

The meaning is that it is the very nature of Śiva. And because this is so, the enjoyer alone—the conscious self—is the grasper who exists eternally and everywhere, in all states such as the various principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), perfectly, without deficiency or excess, in the form of the body, the color blue, and so forth; however, there is no such thing as an object of enjoyment that is separate from the enjoyer. [This applies to] the individual soul (*jīva*).

Beginning with these words and concluding with "Śiva," [the text] teaches by way of a specific method that there is no real difference whatsoever between the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva; thus, one should not consider oneself incomplete in any state such as that of the body, but rather recognize that one's very nature is that of Śiva, who is a mass of consciousness (ciddhana). As it has been said: "Even those who [regard] the body..."

"Those who perceive and worship that which consists of the thirty-six principles as being the very form of Śiva attain perfection; and those who, having likewise resolved upon even an earthen jar or similar object, perceive and worship it as such—they too [attain perfection]. There is no dispute on this point," so it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-Ṭīkā*. Bhaṭṭa Śrī Vāmana has also said:

Since consciousness perceives the object of cognition not by way of its own inherent nature, therefore all that is cognized consists of consciousness; thus, one should become composed of consciousness.

Thus [it is said]. Why is the individual soul (*jīva*) "consisting of all" (*sarvamaya*)? The reason for this is that it is the cause of the emergence—that is, the cause of the production—of all states of being; furthermore, the grammatical designation is primarily intended to express its status as the source (*apādāna*).

Your play (*vihāra*), which consists of the entire collection of distinctions between the knower, the cognition, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, serves here as the cause [of all things].
Since that [illusion] departs from you whenever your expansion ceases, it is therefore never again perceived in this world by anyone through any means whatsoever.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrījñānagarbha-stotra*, since the world exists only when consciousness (*saṃvit*) has emerged, the soul (*jīva*) is the source from which all things arise; and since the universe arises from that very soul, it follows that this [soul] consists of everything and is the power of the universe (*viśvaśakti*). This has been established in the commentary on the second aphorism.

He states another reason for the state of being composed of all (*sarvamayatva*) with the half-verse beginning "in the perception of that" (*tatsaṃvedane*). Because the perception—that is, the manifestation—of all those things such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, is apprehended through the realization of identity with that very form or nature, [it is established that] everything is composed of all. Thus, by these two verses, the secret practices (*rahasyacaryā*) [are explained].

Furthermore, the discourses on the teaching of knowledge, which are constructed as the logical means for uprooting the tree of all dualistic distinctions, have been introduced by the first and last sūtras; the great reality (*mahārthatattva*) by the sūtra concerning the waking state and so forth;

the supreme truth of the Trika system (*ṣaḍardhaparamārtha*) by the sūtra beginning with "having ascended to that"; and the essence of all forms of worship (*sarvopāsāsāra*) and so forth by the subsequent [sūtras].
By means of the very principle of vibration (spandatattva), all instructions regarding the universe have been embraced. || 4 ||

Or rather, for one who possesses the realization that "liberation consists precisely in the essence of this very practice," and for whom the entire world is a play— he who perceives thus, being constantly disciplined, is undoubtedly liberated while living. (5)

The word "vā" (or) indicates that by conceptualizing the manner of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of closing [the senses], which was previously described as the first outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), he suggests the rarity of this attainment. Therefore, the meaning is this: such a consciousness is indeed rare;
it occurs only for someone in their final birth who perceives the entire world as a play (*krīḍā*).

Creating and withdrawing [the universe] through the opening and closing of his own consciousness— O Vaiśya, by means of *māyā*— the great yogi, remaining constantly absorbed in this state according to the teaching of the *Bhagavad Gītā* (12.2), "Those who worship me, ever steadfast," remains thus even while living and possessing vital breaths and the like.

When all bonds have been completely consumed by the fire of consciousness, at the fall of the body, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Śiva himself; if he remains alive, he is liberated through vision alone and is not bound in any way whatsoever. By the phrase "there is no doubt," this is what is implied: liberation [is attained] either through initiation and so forth based on faith in the Guru, or rather, from such knowledge or conduct based solely on one's own realization. || 5 ||
"This very great attainment is the cause for the practitioners, teachers, and others to obtain their desired goal"—
this he states in two verses:
"This alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator."
It is the attainment of identity with that [reality] for the practitioner who so desires. (6)
This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvana, which bestows the true being of Śiva.

Regarding the proclamation that "having become Śiva here, one should worship Śiva," there is no state in the consciousness or perception of the meditator which is not Śiva; this is established for the object of meditation whose nature is Śiva, or for any other specific deity or mantra that serves as the cause for various accomplishments (*siddhi*). Thus, there arises the realization of identity (*ayameda*) with that.

The manifestation [of Śiva] is that state of the practitioner, meditator, teacher, and so forth, which has been established in the form: "There is no state in the contemplation of the word and its meaning which is not Śiva" (2.4). It is the attainment of identity with that [Śiva], an immersion into oneness with Śiva, and not [anything else].

The perception of a form distinct from the five-faced [Śiva] and so forth does not, by mere certainty alone, result in the attainment of identity with that [form]; rather, it occurs for one who desires it— specifically for one who has ascended through the reflective awareness of the will, which consists of the non-conceptual "I-am-ness" (ahantā) that is one with Śiva, the universe.

This is what is meant: for one whose resolve— that "I alone am Śiva, the mass of consciousness and bliss, whose body is the universe, through the realization of identity with that very nature of self-awareness"— bears fruit by becoming free from all conceptual construction (avikalpa-śeṣībhūta), why indeed should the object of meditation, the mantra, the deity, and so forth, not manifest before him?
This is because everything is adhered to by the manifestation of non-duality. As it was said by our venerable Paramagurus:

"O Lord, when the entire interior of the universe is directly composed of Your being, what place is not a field for those possessed of devotion? For whom does the mantra not bear fruit? (Ghaṭakarpara-stotra 1.4).

Thus [it is said]. And this very *samāpatti* (attainment) is the acquisition of the nectar (*amṛta*) whose nature is supreme non-duality; for even when another kind of nectar—which merely bestows firmness upon the body for a limited time—is obtained by practitioners, death must inevitably be encountered. This is the intended meaning of the word "only" (*eva*). In this way...
Throughout [this work], with this very intention, [the author] concludes in the *Śrīsvacchanda*—in the section on the attainment of the nectar (*amṛta*) from the gross perspective—with the statement:
"By means of the yoga of nectar alone, victory over time and death shall occur.
Thus, he sets forth the method for attaining that [nectar] in its ultimate sense.
"Or else, one who abides in the supreme reality is never oppressed at any time," and so forth—
this is the middle [section].
He who always maintains this contemplation is liberated even while living;
time cannot affect him who constantly contemplates Śiva. By means of the yoga of his own will, the yogi moves with a gait that follows his own desire.
"Endowed with the state of *Svacchanda*, he shall attain equality with *Svacchanda*;
being *Svacchanda* indeed, *Svacchanda*, he shall always wander as *Svacchanda*" (7.258).
By means of this composition on the innate (*sahaja*), he was subsequently taught with praise. This very [state] is the grasping of the self.
Regarding that which is called "knowledge"— namely, the instruction that "the Self is to be known"—
this very recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the Self as having the nature of Śiva, who is omniscient, omnipotent, and independent, is what constitutes knowledge;
it is not [any other].
"All this is indeed the Person" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15)—
thus it is declared by those who know the end of the Vedas;
yet all those who worship that [limited] Self do not go to the supreme state (Svacchanda Tantra 4.388).

Thus it is stated in the sacred tradition (āmnāya). Likewise, at the time of initiation, for the purpose of the *yojanikā* and other rites, this very [state] is the grace bestowed upon the disciple’s self; the meaning is that the learned teacher (*ācārya*), knowing this very state of absorption (*samāpatti*), becomes a true teacher by uniting the disciple’s self with Śiva. This [absorption] is established through one's own direct realization for those such as the "spiritual sons" (*putraka*) who have become the very self of Śiva.
The initiation into nirvāṇa bestows the state of true being, which is the ultimate essential nature. As it has been said:
"For one who knows this in its true reality, it bestows (or leads to) nirvāṇa" [the reading *gāminī* is found in the manuscript of the Mūla-Parātrīśikā].
"The initiation becomes undoubtedly devoid of offerings of sesame and clarified butter" (Pañcārthabhāṣya 25).

Regarding this, the venerable and most eminent Great Guru did not employ the restrictive particle *eva* here—meaning that even the initiation pertaining to the Hotṛ priest is indeed initiation—out of the intention that no one should have any lack of confidence in this matter. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the second flow, titled "The Pulsation of the Arising of Innate Knowledge," in the *Spandanirṇaya* composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Kṣemarāja Anaka. 2.
Now, the third outflow (*niṣyanda*):

Thus, the immersion into the reality of vibration (*spandatattva*), which is to be accomplished through the two meditative absorptions of closing and opening the eyes, and which serves as the friction-stick for the emission of both, has been determined by means of the two outflows for the sake of manifesting the state of perfect awakening.
Now, having explained that by means of the practice of this very [mantra] while maintaining control over it, the arising of both supreme and non-supreme manifestations occurs,
and having briefly defined the nature of bondage and liberation, he concludes what was initially undertaken with these nineteen verses beginning with "yatheccha" and ending with "cakreśvaro bhavet."

By means of the third outflow, called the vibration of manifestation (*vibhūtispanda*); therein, with two verses, the sovereignty of the dream state is presented preceded by the illustration of the sovereignty of the perfected ones in the waking state; and with one [verse], stating its opposite, it is said with the intended meaning that constant application alone must be resorted to.

By two [powers], there is the manifestation of knowledge regarding desired objects; by one, the manifestation of the power of agency and the conquest of hunger and other such afflictions; by one, the attainment of omniscience; and by one, the destruction of exhaustion—thus it is described in the group of eight. Thereafter, by one [power], the essential nature of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the vibrating self (*spandātman*) is characterized; by another, [the essential nature of its contraction].
The abandonment of those supernatural powers (*siddhi*) that constitute obstacles to the supreme absorption (*parasamādhi*) has been stated.

By one [verse], the immersion (*samāveśa*) whose nature is the determination of the universal self as the outflow of the second [state] has been described. Then, by one [verse], the method for attaining that state of immersion has been taught. By three [verses], the determination of the bound soul (*paśu*) and the fetters (*pāśa*) has been stated. By one [verse]...
The simultaneous occupation of both the states of bondage and liberation by the *spandatattva* itself has been stated.

Through two [verses], the nature of bondage is reiterated as that which is to be eradicated; through one [verse], which declares the means for its eradication, the meaning taught in the opening sūtra is concluded. This is the summary of the *niḥṣyanda*.

Now the text is being explained. Regarding what was stated—that for one who is "well-awakened" (*suprabuddha*), there is the constant realization of the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*)—therein, by the phrase "constantly exerted," the instruction for the awakened one to practice that [realization] during the waking state is given for the sake of attaining the state of being "well-awakened. This is expressed by the passage beginning with "that state... and so forth.

The destruction of the veil of the yogi’s deep sleep has been described through proficiency in the repeated practice of the means of realization. Now, in order to establish the state of perfect awakening by shattering both worldly dreaming and deep sleep,
and to demonstrate his splendor as appropriate for the dream state, he says:

Just as the Creator, when entreated according to one's desire, brings about for embodied beings the attainment of the objects situated in their hearts by causing the rising of the moon and the sun while they are awake.
Likewise, because he never fails in his affection even for desired objects within a dream,
he who stands in the center must necessarily manifest them most clearly at all times.
He is the Sustainer (*dhātā*) because he sustains everything within himself; he is Śaṅkara’s own nature.

Just as for a waking person whose self-sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is manifested during the state of wakefulness, so it is for the yogi in whom the knowledge residing in the physical body has become manifest precisely within the stage of the body.

Requested by the desire of one who is related [to him], and propitiated by the power of inward-turned self-reflection (*svarūpa-vimarśa*), he accomplishes within the heart— that is, in the mind— the purposes consisting of the arousal, the manifestation of intuition, the movement, and the stabilization of consciousness, preceded by the knowledge of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, regarding the objects situated therein.

How is it that, having brought about the emergence of the moon and the sun— the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*)— that which is illumined by the power of knowledge is indeed manifested by each respective power of action?

This occurs through the expansion of the powers of knowledge and action, which are intensified by the method of firm grounding in the root, consisting of the flash of intuition (*pratibhā*) as it unfolds within the state of immersion (*samāveśa*).

The Supreme Lord, having entered the body of the yogin, brings about this accomplishment. And just as it is so, when sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has perished, that state accessible to the mind is reached, and the Supreme Goddess shines forth. (Vijñānabhairava 75)
Thus,
having meditated upon the power (śakti) as both full and weak within the twelvefold field of perception,
and having entered the heart while meditating, one attains the sovereignty of dream. [Viṇāśikhatantra 55]

Thus, according to the established tradition, for one who does not transgress the eternal *praṇava* by means of the reflective awareness of the power of consciousness— the source of both emissions (*visarga*)— which is intent upon both vomiting and swallowing, and who is devoted to the prayer to the Lord while established in yogic sleep;

The Creator, abiding in the midst of the *suṣumṇā* channel in a most manifest and unobscured form, necessarily reveals— even in dreams— only those desired objects of inquiry, such as the *āṇava*, *śākta*, and *śāmbhava* absorptions (*samāveśa*), as well as others, to one whose mirror of the intellect has been polished by the savor of practicing these absorptions.

The meaning is that this yogin does not experience delusion during the states of dreaming or deep sleep; by the mention of "dreaming," the state of "deep sleep" (sauṣupta) is also implied. In this regard, regarding the manifestation of the desired object, this very [state] is the cause through repetition.

Because the Lord does not transgress the grace (*prasāda*)— characterized by the subsiding of the turbidity of *māyā*— which is produced through the worship consisting of the internal contemplation of one's own nature, which is the very essence of longing and petition. For the Supreme Lord, whose self is consciousness,
certainly brings about whatever is sought through the sequence of service appropriate for the inward-turned state, as if remaining ever-awake.

This should be explained through the use of *śleṣa* (punning) as referring both to one who is awake regarding the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and to one who is situated in the waking state (*jāgarāvasthā*). || 2 ||
If, however, one is not thus attentive, then one does not possess the state of a yogi; so it is said:
"Otherwise, however, creation would be independent because of its inherent nature, just as for an ordinary person in the two states of waking and dreaming. (3)
If the Sustainer is not constantly propitiated through reasoned logic, then, in the absence of abiding in one's own true nature,

the supreme Lordly power— which has as its essential nature the manifestation and ascertainment of common and uncommon objects during both waking and dreaming— will belong to this yogi just as it does to an ordinary person every single day.
The meaning is that if creation were independent, it would cause even the yogin to fall into the pit of saṃsāra, just like ordinary worldly beings; as it has been said:
"The activity of beings is governed by the Lord."
Thus: "Because it possesses that nature" means that in the manifestation of states such as dreaming and waking, the creation of the Lord proceeds from His nature of absolute freedom. || 3 ||

Having thus established the means for dissolving the states of dream and deep sleep for the sake of one's own awakening, he now describes the means for entering the reality of *spanda* (vibration) for the fully awakened one, preceded by illustrations and logical arguments,
and instructs that the realization of the sought-after truth also occurs in this manner.
For just as an object seen indistinctly, even when the mind is attentive, appears much more clearly once it has been cultivated through the exertion of its own power. (4)
Thus, whatever exists in its ultimate sense, by what means, where, and in what manner— that very thing, having been mastered by power, proceeds forth before long exactly as it is.

The word *hi* has the sense of *kila*. Even when the mind is attentive, an object—due to defects such as distance—may indeed be seen indistinctly; yet, through repeated direct observation characterized by the exertion of its own power, it is intensely contemplated and thoroughly perceived, so that it does not merely appear clear, but appears even more clearly. In the same way, that power which consists of the essence of *spanda*...

That which exists as the agent—by means of that essence consisting of a mass of bliss (*ānandaghana*) in its ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), wherein [it resides] within the self-nature of Śaṅkara; "as" (meaning) by way of non-dual pervasion (*abhedavyāpti*);
and "thus" (meaning) it is brought about through the exertion of its own power, namely, through the effort of cultivating the state of being one with that [reality] by turning inward.

It proceeds and becomes manifest very swiftly and with extreme clarity. How? By having first seized the plane of the limited subject—the imagined body and so forth—of the worshiper and having caused it to be submerged within one's own self; and furthermore, by having seized the power whose nature is vibration (*spanda*) while remaining established therein.
For the practitioner-yogin who repeatedly pierces through the ground of the subject constituted by the imagined body and intellect,

whatever he desires to know— such as a treasure— and in whatever place, by whatever material such as gold, in its ultimate reality, and in whatever configuration it exists, that very thing is revealed to him without delay. || 5 ||
He states that even the power of the agent and so forth arises from this very force:
"Since even a weak person, having overcome it [the power], proceeds to action;
and likewise, one who is extremely hungry might suppress his hunger. (6)

Just as one whose vital essence is exhausted and who is like a sage, by seizing the power that consists of vibration (*spanda*), repeatedly energizes the level of the subject consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the force of the immersion into vibration (*spandasamāveśa*),
and thus engages in a task that must necessarily be performed— even an impossible object— precisely by means of that seizure of power.

The meaning is that he performs [these actions]. Likewise, even one who is afflicted by hunger and thirst pacifies such hunger, thirst, and so forth through the conquest of that power. Indeed, for one who has entered the ground (bhūmi) which is a mass of consciousness (ciddhana), there is no subjugation by dualities whatsoever; for that [subjugation] rests only upon the plane of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, and that [plane] is submerged here in this ground of consciousness. || 6 ||
Since such a collection of accomplishments arises from this [power] according to the sequence of scriptural authority and logical proof thus stated, therefore:
"Just as omniscience and other qualities exist when [the power] presides over the body, so too will it be everywhere by virtue of its presiding over one's own self. (7)

When the body is presided over— that is, pervaded— by this principle of *spanda*, which is the very essence of one's own nature, then just as the attributes of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth arise for the embodied being through the instruments of experiencing objects appropriate to that state, so too, if this [power] were to withdraw everything like the contraction of a tortoise’s limbs...

Alternatively, by means of the logic of great expansion (*mahāvikāsa-yukti*), one effects an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) within one's own imperishable self, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).

Having recognized that very [self] through the aforementioned higher knowledge (*abhijñāna*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), one establishes a state of immersion (*samāveśa-sthiti*) therein. Then, "everywhere"—that is, from Śiva down to the earth—one becomes thus: namely, of the nature of Śaṅkara, possessing the appropriate omniscience and omnipotence, and so forth.
It will come to pass. || 7 ||
He says that this too is by His grace:
"Languor is a plunderer of the body, and its course proceeds from ignorance;
if it is destroyed by the unfolding of that [consciousness], how could it exist without a cause? (8)
By implication, for a person who identifies with the body, that loss of joy is *vuluṇṭhikā*—
it bestows the wretchedness of limitation by robbing one of the wealth of supreme consciousness.
And from that exhaustion arises rebirth, which occurs due to ignorance— the failure to recognize one’s own true nature as a mass of consciousness and bliss.

Then, that exhaustion is cut away; because the cause—the non-knowledge of the Self—is absent, how could it remain? It would not exist. And in the absence of exhaustion, even the states of suffering such as disease, which are inevitable in the body, are progressively removed from the yogi, just as dross is removed from gold being intensely heated.

When darkness has departed, one's own true nature indeed shines forth intensely. And thus, for the supreme yogin, the constant absence of fatigue even while remaining in the body is a supernatural power (*vibhūti*). As it was said by the supreme yoginī Madālāsā while employing young children as her instruments:
Do not fall into delusion regarding this body of yours, which is like a garment to be cast off;
for this body has been bound to you as a garment by auspicious and inauspicious karmas, by intoxication and other such passions. (Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya 25.14)

Thus, it has also been established by the Blessed One that for a yogin desiring the attainment of the measured [powers], through the practice of absorption (*samāveśa*), piercing the body leads to victory over diseases such as wrinkles and gray hair. || 8 ||

Now, regarding the inquiry as to what the nature of this "unfolding" (unmeṣa) is and by what means it is attained, he says: "That which arises for one intent upon a single thought is to be known as unfolding;
one should perceive it for oneself. (9)
"Once mental objects have been abandoned, consciousness, being restrained, does not go toward another object;
then, by means of that intermediate state, the meditation on the supreme reality expands.
According to this principle (*Viśvabhairava-tantra* 62), within a certain state of contemplation whose nature consists of stilling fluctuations through a specific focal point—

For the yogin who is intensely absorbed and one-pointed, because it is "restrained" (*yata*), there arises from the Spanda-principle— which is non-dual with Agni and Soma— the lower [state] characterized by the expansion of consciousness shining forth through the excellence of that one-pointedness, due to the closing of the objective support and the sudden swallowing of the entire stream of thoughts.
Thus, this arising, which consists of the wonder of consciousness, would be a distinct, supramundane radiance;

that [arising] should be understood and sought as "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*) precisely because it is the cause of the unfolding of that wonder. It can be known by the yogi only in this way; and therefore, [it is said to be] "by itself."

Because it lacks the objectivity of "this-ness" (idantā), one should perceive it within oneself by means of the "I-ness" (ahantā) itself—through an attentiveness that is uncreated and characterized by effort—and recognize it through its unique nature as wonder (camatkāra). For when one is engaged in the contemplation of one object, such as the investigation of an external thing, there occurs the sudden emergence of another thought. That [emergence]...
Others say that *unmeṣa* (the unfolding) is that which pervades the two types of thought. || 9 ||

Now, he instructs that even those various accomplishments (siddhis), which are attainable through the exertion of practitioners of limited yoga and arise merely from the cultivation of the upward breath (unmeṣa), must be regarded as things to be abandoned by the supreme yogin; thus:
"From this [comes] the point (bindu), from this the sound (nāda), from this the form, and from this the taste."
They set in motion, in no time at all, embodied beings by means of agitation. || 10 ||

From this unfolding (unmeṣa), which is being perceived, for the yogin whose sense of "I-ness" regarding the gross and subtle bodies and so forth does not dissolve, there arises in the space between the eyebrows and other locations a point (bindu) in the form of the light of the star,
and the sound (nāda), which consists of the light of the totality of all objects of knowledge.
The form [of the deity] consists of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*), which is the undifferentiated word-form that expresses everything; the light is the illumination even in darkness;
and the taste is the transcendent savor at the tip of the tongue.

These exist as the agitators [of the senses], serving as obstacles to the attainment of the principle of vibration (*spanda-tattva*), yet they provide satisfaction insofar as they [initially] obstruct it. As they have said:
"These are obstacles in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), but accomplishments (*siddhi*) upon emergence" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 3.37).

Thus, it has been stated that even for a yogi who is intent on observing the unfolding [of consciousness] yet still identifies the body as the self, the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth become causes of agitation. || 10 ||

Now, he says that within this very nature which consists of unmesha (the unfolding of consciousness), one immerses the state of being a limited embodied subject and attains even the state of the supreme subject, whose form is that [unmesha]: "When,
as if out of a desire to see, one remains pervading all objects..."
Then, what is the use of much speaking? One will understand it for oneself. || 11 ||
Just as at the moment of the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*), the object sought to be seen flashes forth internally in its differentiated forms for one who perceives in the state of *paśyantī*,

in the same way, [the subject] pervades all objects— beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva— as taught in the cosmological systems (*adhvaprakriyā*) of the *Svacchanda* and other scriptures; thus, like Sadāśiva, he thinks, "I am everything."

When one remains, having covered [the mind] by embracing within it the non-dual reflective awareness (*abheda-vimarśa*) which culminates in the absence of conceptualization (*avikalpa*), preceded by the continuous flow of one's own mental constructs (*svavikalpānusandhāna*); as long as one does not waver from this meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), there arises the state of the Great Subject (*mahā-pramātṛtā*), which swallows all objects of knowledge by unifying them with the Self.
One's own self-awareness alone will experience this; what is the use of much exposition on this matter? || 11 ||

Having asserted that its perception is "constant," it is subsequently established that for one who practices the collection of means explained immediately thereafter, the state of being perpetually immersed in the reality of *spanda* arises for the well-awakened one;
this occurs within the heart of the disciple because it is inseparable from that infinite object of knowledge.
Recalling [the previous teaching] by way of a concluding summary on the method of entry, he says:
"Awakened, one should always remain having perceived the field of experience through knowledge;
one should unify everything in that one place, and thereafter one is not afflicted by anything else. (12)

One should remain ever awakened throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as at the beginning, middle, and end of consciousness; with divine vision established through the support of the reality of *spanda* (vibrant vitality) which has been unveiled, one should attain the state of perfect awakening. How so?
Through knowledge, by means of outward-turned manifestation, everything within the field of perception—whether in the form of blue, pleasure, or other objects—is [revealed].
Having observed the sensory object,

and having reflected according to the perspective established by the statement, "There is no state in which she is not Śiva during the contemplation of word and meaning" (2.4), [one should rest] in that single creative source, the essential nature whose self is Śaṅkara.
One should project everything [into consciousness] and know it as non-different during both the states of closing and opening [the eyes];

by means of the firmness of support from the preceding and succeeding limits, one should perceive even the middle ground as nothing other than the solidification of the essence of consciousness (cid-rasa). And thus, there is nothing else whatsoever that is separate [from it].
In every case, [the individual] is sublated by the objective entity, because everything has been accepted as one's own self. As it was said by the venerable author of the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"O Lord, he who perceives this entire circle of objects as free from conceptual construction sees it as Your very body."
When the world has been completely filled by his own self, how can there be any fear for him who is eternally blissful? (Uttara-stotra 13) || 12 ||

Regarding what was stated— that "one is not afflicted by another"— an objection may arise as to who this "other" afflictor is and who the afflicted is, since it has been declared that the entire universe is of the nature of Śiva. Anticipating this, he speaks in order to determine the true nature of the bonds (pāśas) and the bound soul (paśu).
Having become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds (the alphabet),
and with his sovereign power eclipsed by *kalā*, he is known as a bound soul (*paśu*).

In this context, that very nature of Śiva which has been described as the essence of light is established; this Lord, the cause of the universe, performs creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace. (Svacchanda Tantra)
Thus, according to the perspective of the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra*, He who is eternally embraced by His own power (*nija-śakti*),

performing the fivefold cosmic acts (*pañcavidha-kṛtya*) as the independent Lord, is celebrated in the Āgamas by such names as Spanda, Lalita, Īśvara, and so forth. His very power of freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which is eternal and consists of the nature of the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), is the supreme Great Being (*mahāsattā*) known as Matsyodarī.

She is defined in various places through countless modes, such as "the throbbing wave," "the essence," "the heart," "Bhairavī the Goddess," and "the crest-lock. Indeed, she is the very fullness of consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*), who,
having embraced the noble letters from *a* to *kṣa* by means of the encapsulation of the unsurpassed, unstruck power (*anuttarānāhataśakti*), is therefore [the source].

The Supreme Speech (Parā Vāk) is that which consists of the Great Mantra—eternally arisen and unutterable—which is the very nature of uninterrupted reflective awareness; it is the life-force of all, the wheel of all powers whose expansion comprises the six paths in the form of infinite signifieds and signifiers that have been internalized, and it is the succession of all creations, dissolutions, and so forth. Such is the Lord’s [Supreme Speech].

Because it vibrates (*spandate*) while manifesting within itself, as it were, the movement of this manifold variety of the universe— following the etymological derivation of the word— it is here called *spanda*. And thus, the Blessed One, who is beautiful through the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) inlaid with all these powers of the universe, manifests upon the very wall of his own self, part by part, in the play of concealing his own true nature.
To the extent that She desires to act, Her own power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), though singular and undivided, assumes the state of will (*icchātva*).
Abiding in the form of knowledge and action, She becomes twofold through the distinction between the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*), which consist of the reflective awareness of Śiva and Śakti.
Then, manifesting through the divisions of the consonant groups and the divisions of their respective phonetic energies (*kalā*), She vibrates ninefold and fiftyfold.

Manifesting through forms that consist of the deities of consciousness— whose essence is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) [of the Lord], and which range from non-terrible to terrible to most terrible— the Lord’s performance of the fivefold cosmic act (*pañcavidhakṛtya*) is accomplished. As it is said in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:

"That power of the Creator of the world which is said to be inherent—when He desires to emit [the universe], that Goddess assumes the nature of His will. Listen now to how, though she is one, she comes to possess multiplicity. (3.5)
It should be known with perfect certainty that "it is thus" and not otherwise.
When she makes known [the will] here in this world, saying "let all this be so," and is oriented toward action, she is called the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
When that very object is produced at that very moment, the activity of producing it is what is called "action" (kriyā).
In this way, although action has only two forms, it attains infinity through further subdivisions.
Under the influence of the limiting adjuncts of objects, the Sovereign Goddess becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem;
having first entered therein into the state of the Mother, she then manifests in her various forms.
The Mālinī [alphabet] is twofold, ninefold, and fiftyfold;
it is twofold due to the division into seeds (bīja) and wombs (yoni). The vowels are considered to be the seeds.
The consonants beginning with *ka* are traditionally held to have ninefold origins according to the division of their classes;
through the distinct classification of the vowels to be excluded, they shine with fifty rays of light.
The seed-syllable is Śiva, and the womb is said to be Śakti;
this is to be known as the eight groups (varga) in sequence, beginning with Aghora.
That very [power], through its differentiation of energies, constitutes the eightfold group beginning with Māheśvarī;
and when divided into fifty varieties, O fair-faced one, it possesses that same number.
The Supreme Lord has conceived [these letters] as the designators of the Rudras,
and likewise, in their proper sequence, as the designators of the Śaktis who are equal in number to them.

And so forth. Likewise, those [energies] which, being devoid of Rudra and extremely terrible, bind the conscious beings to the objects themselves and cause their lives to fall lower and lower; others, however, are even more fearsome.
Attached to the wheel of mixed karma, they are like the nine vajras as before;
those bonds, which obstruct the path to liberation, are both supreme and inferior.

"As previously [stated], those supreme Aghora Śiva-powers, which bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva upon the multitude of living beings, have been described by the knowers of that [reality]. (3.33) Thus, from the Mass of Sounds (Śabdarāśi) has arisen the group of deities beginning with Brāhmī, consisting of nine classes (vargas).

Being perceived as the object of enjoyment by Him who is accompanied by Śiva, that very nature whose essence is Śaṅkara is known as the *paśu* (bound soul) in the Āgamas; thus it is stated therein. Now, to pacify the doubt as to how the Great Lord, the enjoyer (*bhoktā*), could have reached this state, he states the reason by means of a qualification:

Regarding the phrase *kalāviluptavibhavaḥ*: "Kalā" is the power of *māyā*, so called because it "measures" (*kalayati*), casts outward, and delimits by means of limitation. The meaning is that his glory has been eclipsed by that [power]; he remains with his sovereignty concealed by his own *māyā*. Furthermore, by "kalā," there is intended the power whose nature is to reinforce limited agency, as characterized by that [term].
"His power is obscured by the veil consisting of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *niyati*, and *rāga*;

his attributes such as fullness and agency are concealed. To the question, "Let this be so; but how has he come to become the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatā*) for the group of powers (*śakti-varga*)," this very point is the answer.

My power has been eclipsed by the *kalās*—the presiding deities of the groups of letters beginning with 'A', such as Brāhmī and the rest—and by those phonemes beginning with 'A'. Thus contracted and incomplete, I think: "I shall do this; I shall take up this; I shall abandon this."
Since he does not attain a state of his own essential nature— which is neither gross nor subtle— having entered into a multitude of various conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions such as these,
he is therefore called a *paśu* (bound soul), being consumed by the group of powers (*śakti*) in the manner described above, through the power of *kalā*.

Through the aspect of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), its power is obscured and it appears as if contracted, yet in reality, its nature as Śiva has never departed anywhere; for in the absence of that [manifestation], it itself would not shine forth. Thus, by means of the limited powers (*kalā*), words, and cognitions that appear in such a way, its power is obscured and it does not perceive itself as being of that [contracted] form.
The meaning is that he is capable of reflecting upon it. || 13 ||
Now, he analyzes the bound soul (*paśu*), who is constrained by the limited power of vision and is subject to fetters:

"The emergence of a cognition in him, which results in the loss of the essence of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*), causes him to fall into a state of lack of autonomy; and that [cognition] has as its object only those [limited] elements (*tanmātra*). (14)

The emergence—the birth tainted by destruction—of those perceptions of that animal, which consist of worldly and scriptural conceptualizations and are the arising of conceptual cognitions of diverse objects permeated by them; that is the loss, the submergence, of the supreme nectar-essence, the mass of consciousness, the expansion of bliss. When these [perceptions] have arisen...
Although the ground of consciousness remains present even amidst cognitions of diverse objects, it appears as if non-existent because it is not being reflected upon;
for this reason, it has been stated thus. And by the arising of these cognitions, this [consciousness] attains a state of lack of autonomy and becomes subject to their power.
As it is said in the *Śrī Śivasūtras*: "Knowledge is bondage" (1.2).
The venerable sage Vyāsa has also said: "In childhood, one is composed of mother and father. And the venerable Ālasya has said:
"One thinks 'father' to some extent, 'son' to some extent, 'beloved' to some extent, 'mine' to some extent, and 'not mine' to some extent; do not speak in many ways of this deluded multitude."
(Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 25.15).

The meaning is that [the state] has as its object a distinct knowable thing (*vedya*), being such that its scope consists of the emergence of cognition (*pratyaya*)—namely, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—which function as generalities through the distinctions of intense and very intense degrees. By this, he says the following: as long as this...

As long as there is the manifestation of diverse objects of cognition, one is indeed bound; however, when, through the reasoning of the aforementioned instruction, one realizes with unwavering conviction that everything is composed of the Self alone, then one is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*). As it has been said:
"Or he whose consciousness... (2.5), and so forth. And thus, that which was stated previously—

Therefore, there is no state in the contemplation of word and meaning that is not Śiva; (2.4) and so forth—there is no slight discrepancy between this [statement] and the verse: "There is no loss of the supreme nectar-essence along with him, which arises from cognition" (3.14). 14.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If even the emergence of cognition results in the loss of this [consciousness] of the supreme nectar-essence, then how can it be said that he has become the object of enjoyment for the group of powers? To dispel this doubt, [the author] says:
"And his powers are perpetually active in veiling his own nature."
For there is no arising of cognition without the interpenetration of words. || 15 ||
The particle *ca* indicates a doubt and conjoins another point that serves as its resolution:

although this form of the animal— which is one's own nature as Śiva— is manifest as the foundational substratum (*bhittibhūta*) for its concealment, when it is not correctly reflected upon (*samyag-aparāmarśane*), the powers whose nature has been explained arise constantly on account of that [concealment].

For as long as the recognition of his own true nature— which consists of the essence of the supreme nectar— has not occurred for him, these [powers] continue to exert themselves to veil that true nature; because whatever emergence of cognition in him—
the flow of conceptual and non-conceptual knowledge— is permeated by words in such forms as "I know this."

Since it does not exist without being colored by subtle internal sounds and without association with gross verbal expressions, even animals possess an internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of sound— which, though non-conventional, resembles a designation for themselves and resembles the designation "head"— in the form of an internal acceptance; otherwise, [it would not be possible].

The initial grasping of linguistic conventions by an infant would not be possible, because [the infant's cognition] is devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of internal inclusion (*ūha*) and exclusion (*apoha*). However, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which consists of the interpenetration with gross linguistic elements, is established for everyone through one's own experience. (15)
Concluding the meaning expressed in these three verses, and maintaining the previously stated non-difference of the object of knowledge from the universal principle of vibration (spanda),
he characterizes bondage and liberation as consisting respectively in the non-recognition and recognition of that [principle].
This very power of Śiva, whose nature is action, resides within the bound soul (paśu). When it remains on its own path, it is the binder; when known, it brings about accomplishment.
