Because she has been determined by the three preceding verses, she— shining forth in the form that extends to the objects of knowledge— is the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) herself, whose essence is the *spanda* principle and who belongs to Śiva, the conscious Self whose nature is one's own essential being; for she is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), since she effects the establishment of the manifold variety of the universe.
According to the previously established view, while [the limited subject] exists having assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu) within Śiva alone,
she— acting as the agent by sprinkling this [limited self], which consists of the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), with a drop of the "I-consciousness" (ahantā)—
fails to recognize it in its true form.

Because it conceals one's true nature and because it is the cause of the afflictions of taking up and casting off [objects], it becomes the binder. But when there is the contemplation without division of the path of one's own Śiva-nature— that is, for one who has entered the state of Śakti— then [it becomes the liberator].
"Then he becomes the very form of Śiva; this is called the face of Caivī.

(20) According to the principle stated by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka, when the yogi realizes that this power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is identical with that supreme power (*parāśakti*), which is the means of attainment, or when [he realizes] the nature of Śiva even amidst the flow of both conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions—

When the entirety of the knowable, which is indeed a portion of one's own self, is perceived by this [means], then it brings about for him that supreme perfection consisting of supreme bliss. || 17 ||
(Thus demonstrating that the bound soul (*paśu*) is bound in this manner and is liberated through the cultivation of the means to be described hereafter,
he restates the nature of bondage as something to be eradicated: "By means of that which consists of the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), residing in the mind, ego, and intellect..."
Constrained by the city of eight, he experiences that which arises from the resulting cognitions. [The commentary for this verse was not found. || 17 ||
He experiences enjoyment under the control of another; because of that state, he wanders in saṃsāra.
Therefore, we shall now explain the cause for the dissolution of this saṃsāra.

He experiences enjoyment arising from the *puryaṣṭaka*. Precisely because the emergence of cognitions such as pleasure occurs within the objective manifestations (*pratyaya*), for that very reason this bound soul (*paśu*) is dependent on another due to the arising of those cognitions; being drawn along step by step by the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī through the process of the permeation of sound, he is not independent like one who is perfectly awakened. His [state] is thus.

Precisely because of the existence of the *puryaṣṭaka*, its various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are repeatedly awakened; thus it wanders through transmigration, acquiring and then discarding bodies that serve as suitable substrates for various experiences.
Since this is so, that which is the most excellent [aspect] of the transmigration of this [self] when it is confined within the *puryaṣṭaka*—

"Laya" (dissolution) is destruction through the eradication of the impurity consisting of the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*); we shall explain its cause, which is a truly easy means, immediately hereafter—we shall set it forth in this treatise, having established it ourselves. [The use of the present tense] "we explain" (*saṃpracakṣmahe*) is justified by the rule that the present may be used for what is proximate to the present (*vartamāna-sāmīpye*).
Thus, there is the usage of the present tense according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.131. || 18 ||
Establishing this, he concludes the meaning stated in the first sūtra:

"But when [the practitioner] is firmly established in one [deity], then by controlling its dissolution and emergence, he attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, he becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara). (19)

Furthermore, when this [practitioner], having cultivated the methods of instruction for immersion into the supreme reality (*paratattva*), becomes firmly established and absorbed in the single principle of *spanda*— which is the self of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*)—

and thus becomes identical with it, then, by means of that very [principle], [he attains] that [state] of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) previously mentioned in the preceding sūtra, and likewise of the universe.
By means of the two absorptions of closing and opening, he governs dissolution and emergence;
through the perspective established by the first aphorism, performing both withdrawal and creation from the single essential nature of Śaṅkara,
he attains the state of the enjoyer by swallowing the entire range of objects of enjoyment, from the earth up to Śiva.

One relies upon the very reality of supreme subjectivity through the process of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Consequently, one becomes the Lord (*īśvara*) of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which is the collection of one's own rays as determined in the first aphorism.
By this very body, one indeed attains the state of the Great Lord (*maheśvaratva*); such is the meaning. Thus...

By demonstrating the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*) of the great meaning between the beginning and the conclusion, the illustrious teacher Vasugupta reveals that this scripture is the crown jewel of all the Upaniṣads of Śaṅkara, owing to its essential core. Thus, may there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the third flow, the Spanda of Manifestations, in the venerable Spandanirṇaya.
Now, the fourth outflow: at the end of the text, he praises the supreme stage of vibration (*spandabhūmi*) and the Guru’s speech through a punning expression:
"She who is the boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt."
I pay homage to that wondrous speech of the Guru, which is variegated with words of manifold meanings.
According to the established principle stated in the *Vijñānabhairava* (20)— "The Goddess who is the commonality of all darkness is here called the mouth of the Guru"—
she is the form of the Teacher (*ācārya*), as she is the cause for attaining the abode of Śiva. Furthermore,
because she encompasses the levels of speech beginning with *paśyantī*, she is the Great Speech (*mahatī bhāratī*), the supreme Word (*parā vāk*), as well as the Guru, the Teacher.

I bow to— that is, I enter with the recognition of her absolute preeminence— the speech of the Teacher which is connected [to the Truth], variegated, and consisting of world-transcending wonder; and furthermore, because its essential nature flashes forth in all states,
I salute it as if it were speaking, through the effort of its own arising power.

I bring face to face that state which culminates in the reflective awareness of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-vimarśa*), so that I may enter into it. Of what sort is it? It is the ferryboat for the complete crossing of the vast ocean of doubt—that very ocean being the manifold stain of suspicion consisting of a deep and insurmountable uncertainty born from the absence of the certainty of perfect self-identity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā-niścaya*).

The phrase "like a boat" (*nauriva tām*) is to be applied to both cases. Likewise, that supreme speech in which there are words (*padāni*)—that is, poetic pauses (*viśrāntayaḥ*)—whose meanings are manifold (*vicitrārthāni*), serving the purpose of various aesthetic wonders;
or that speech of the Guru in which there are "meaning-words" (*arthapadāni*), that is, the signified and the signifier, entered into a beautiful composition (*ramyaracanā*). || 1 ||

By uttering his own name, whose power is well-known, the author of the treatise inspires confidence in those seeking [the truth] and, through the necessity of concealment, demonstrates the great fruitfulness of this scripture: "Even having obtained this wealth of knowledge— which is otherwise difficult to attain— [it remains] deposited within the cave of the heart."
For, like Vasugupta, he always brings about the welfare of the entire world. || 2 ||
This very knowledge, declared in this scripture, is the cause for attaining the goal of human existence;

having obtained it— though it is difficult to attain and hard to acquire— and having received from the surface of the stone the essence of Śaṅkara’s instruction in a dream, one realizes that the Heart itself, consisting of Light and Awareness, is within the universe.

Because it provides entry and space, it is a cave; within that cave, he has made a definitive deposit— that is, a placement— of that very wealth of knowledge belonging to its owner, the Guru named Śrī Vasugupta, in such a way that it became for his own benefit.

In the same way, because there is no restriction on eligibility, it leads to eternal Śiva for anyone in the world who, through effort not limited by conventional time, conceals [the teaching] within the heart and makes it one's own through firm realization.
It is for the sake of attaining immersion into one's own essential nature, which is eternally identical with Śaṅkara, that this [treatise] is accomplished; may there be auspiciousness. || 2 ||
Although there is indeed no counting of commentaries in this treatise, and although people in this world are for the most part of a superficial disposition,
even those who are skilled will recognize the distinction of our explanation.
Some are royal swans of consciousness, skilled in extracting the essence. || 1 ||
Because he could not tolerate [the work] remaining among the infinite other commentators, the Spandaśāstra was explained by our Guru, and not by me; yet, [it remains here] for his sake.
A slight indication of the distinction was shown previously in the *Sandoha*; today, however, [it concerns] one who possesses the immersion into the power of Rudra and is of the nature of Śiva.
At the intense request of his own disciple named Śūra, this was determined by Kṣemarāja from the vast [teachings] of his supreme Guru. || 4 ||
Those whose intellect has not been clarified by the instructions of true teachers regarding the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the illustrious Śiva-scripture, whose delusion has not been shattered,
and those of dull wit who have never before tasted the nectar of the *Pratyabhijñā*— they are not qualified for this work.
Let this, moreover, be savored by others whose intentions are fulfilled. || 5 ||

Victorious is that supreme vibration of consciousness, from which this entire universe— this vast and expansive manifestation of the path (adhvan) extending from Śiva down to the earth, its body variegated by the states of manifold creation, maintenance, and dissolution— is but a tiny particle of its own unfolding.
The ground that is the abode of the bliss of the ten senses. || 6 ||
This *Śrīspandanirṇaya* is completed;
it is the work of Śrī Kṣemarāja, who received instruction from the Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Śrīmad Abhinavaguptanātha, the grand-pupil of the author of the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*. May there be auspiciousness!
By the command of the illustrious King Pratāpa, this [work] has been prepared and published by Madhusūdana Kaul for the delight of the virtuous.
